_note: A database, not a page. Three orthogonal axes. KIND = what it is (term/person/work/study/event/mechanism/case). LANE = what it does: application, consideration or manipulation. The ten sections ask WHERE (fandom, sport, AI, brands); the lanes ask WHY anyone is using it. A fan club is application; the same fan club with a paid tier is manipulation; the study of both is consideration. verified=false means the ENTRY is real and the CITATION needs checking - filter /encyclopedia/?unverified=1 is the work queue. SECTIONS = which of the ten site sections an entry also belongs to, so each section has its own timeline.

application.name: Application
application.blurb: One-sided attachment put to work on purpose. Creator economies, community, fandom as infrastructure, and the things that genuinely help people. Not automatically good - a tool with an obvious use is a tool that will also get a bad one.

consideration.name: Consideration
consideration.blurb: The part where somebody stops and thinks. The research, the diagnosis, the ethics, the lawsuits, the regulators. Roughly fifty years of arguing with itself about whether this is a relationship.

manipulation.name: Manipulation
manipulation.blurb: One-sided attachment engineered for somebody else's benefit. Paid intimacy, parasocial persuasion, sasaeng, grief extraction, the streak. The lane that pays the bills and the lane that causes the most harm, frequently at the same time.

entries.title: The dog
entries.summary: The first domesticated animal, attached to one particular ape for at least fifteen thousand years and probably rather longer: how long ago exactly is not settled, and the genomic estimates disagree by a factor of two.
entries.significance: Not the origin, and not one-sided: a dog is not a figure and it answers back. What is unique here is that this is the one bond on this site that was bred - the first relationship humans built by selecting for it rather than inventing it, which is why every later version is compared to it and why the comparison keeps being fair. Everything invented since either copies the deal (attention on a schedule, an unchanging face, a fixed voice) or breaks the only clause the dog kept: that the other end is actually there. The people who came before it - the dead kept within reach, the animals carved with human gestures - are not weaker versions of this. They are a different fact, and this site had the order wrong.

sources.citation: Parker, H. G., & Gilbert, S. F. (2015). From caveman companion to medical innovator: genomic insights into the origin and evolution of domestic dogs. Advances in Genomics and Genetics, 5, 239-255. doi:10.2147/AGG.S57678
sources.claim: The timing is genuinely unsettled and the paper says so rather than rounding it. Fossils more similar to modern dogs date to 14,000-17,000 years ago; whole-genome divergence estimates run 13,000-32,000 years ago and mtDNA anywhere from 5,400 to over 100,000; the authors place the actual domestication 'somewhere in between 15,000 and 30,000 ya'. On what was selected for: the behavioural genes under selection are response to stress, fear and defence, and a reduced fear response is offered as a candidate driver of domestication - not attachment itself. Fox selection experiments are cited as showing phenotypic change is achievable within twenty generations under selection for tameness.

entries.title: The story told again
entries.summary: Myths are not stories people tell once. They are stories with a fixed shape that get told to the same audience on a schedule.
entries.significance: The oldest *written-down* schedule in this catalogue: fixed, repeatable, known in advance, and useless for anything except the purpose it was made for. Everything after is a variant. It is not the oldest attachment here - neanderthal-burial and paleolithic-figures sit tens of thousands of years earlier - but it is the earliest one we can read, which is a different and lesser claim than the one this entry used to make.

sources.claim: The deep structure this site keeps rediscovering, from a source far older than fandom: Victor Turner's account of ritual and communitas, in which people temporarily become equal in a shared symbolic space and the intensity of that experience is the point
sources.citation: Turner, V. W. (1969). The Ritual Process: Structure and Meaning.

sources.claim: Campbell's monomyth is the version everyone cites and it is the least reliable part of the package - worth saying so, since the site should not smuggle a contested framework in as settled
sources.citation: Campbell, J. (1949). The Hero with a Thousand Faces.

entries.title: Pygmalion
entries.summary: The sculptor who fell in love with his own work. The statue was never going to be able to leave, and the story treats that as part of the appeal rather than a tragedy to be corrected.
entries.significance: Not the origin - the archaeology in this file runs tens of thousands of years further back, and Roman wax imagines predate Ovid by two and a half centuries. What this is: the first time the structure was written down deliberately, by a Roman, as a story worth telling about a man who loved something that could not leave. The telling detail was never that he loved a statue. It was that the statue was never going to be able to leave, and that this seems to have been part of the appeal. The feeling is real and entirely structured around the other party's inability to reciprocate, and everyone since has rediscovered it.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Ovid. Metamorphoses, Book X. Published ca. AD 8; Ovid 43 BC - 17/18 AD.

entries.title: The congregation
entries.summary: A regular assembled audience for a figure who addresses them, in a building, on a schedule, for years.
entries.significance: The largest organised parasocial arrangement in history, and the one the field has never taken seriously as one. It has a leader, a schedule, a building, an emotional register, an exegesis tradition and a revenue model.

sources.claim: A fan forum is a functioning community, not a comment box: K-pop stan Twitter operates as a Community of Practice - members form interpersonal bonds, communicate regularly, and contribute in their own capacities
sources.citation: Malik, Z., & Haidar, S. (2020). Online community development through social interaction - K-Pop stan twitter as a community of practice. Interactive Learning Environments, 31(2).

sources.claim: AND THE FINDING NOBODY NOTICES: that community has a power hierarchy among its participants - described by the authors as 'usually the least noticed aspect in research on online platforms'. The folklore of equal fans is empirically false
sources.citation: Malik, Z., & Haidar, S. (2020). Interactive Learning Environments, 31(2).

sources.claim: Why the congregation forms: PSRs develop because they fulfil a need to belong and are maintained through parasocial interaction and fandom activity; the authors conclude they may need redefining because fans perceive reciprocity. N=126 stan / N=111 non-stan / N=12 interviews
sources.citation: Y/N and OOMFs: Development, Maintenance, and Consequences of Parasocial Relationships on Stan Twitter (2024). Asia Social Issues.

sources.claim: The congregation is not a consolation prize. Some fans attributed the friends they most wanted to be close with to their fanship itself
sources.citation: Ascue et al., Annyeong, Saranghae: A Phenomenological Study on the Effects of Parasocial Relationships between Adult Filipino K-pop Fans and their Idols. De La Salle University.

sources.claim: Scale and intensity: 63% of adolescent fans (14-18) agreed or strongly agreed with at least 10 of 20 parasocial interaction scale items, 13% strongly agreed with 15 or more, and 52% reported over two hours a day on their idol's content
sources.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans (explanatory sequential mixed methods, Ontario).

sources.claim: The verdict, in the participants' own words: 'You feel as if you've known them for a long time' - said about an idol sharing his feelings on a livestream
sources.citation: Ascue et al., Annyeong, Saranghae (De La Salle University).

entries.title: The priest
entries.summary: A person who hears the specifics, performs the ritual, and knows the family history, on a repeating cycle.
entries.significance: The most complete parasocial arrangement available and it includes a uniform, a script and a confession. It is also the arrangement the most people are inside of, which is the strongest evidence that the form is universal rather than a symptom.

sources.claim: THE ENTIRE ARGUMENT OF THIS SITE, IN ONE ABSTRACT. Followers turn to priests' social posts for scriptural insight and a sense of connection, yet their engagement rarely extends beyond viewing, liking, sharing and brief thanks. Priests seldom reply, solicit topics, or host real-time dialogue. N=20
sources.citation: Between pulpit and platform: Parasocial bonds in Filipino priests' social media ministry (2025). Taylor's FSLM Journals.

sources.claim: And the finding that indicts the apparatus: the ties REMAIN parasocial - one-sided and deferential - EVEN AS priests adopt influencer cues such as eye-catching thumbnails, follower milestones and donation links. Identical equipment, reciprocity that never arrives
sources.citation: Between pulpit and platform (2025).

sources.claim: Cultivation and harvesting, named as such by someone studying it as evangelism: seven pastors using YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok use the same techniques as secular influencers to cultivate PSRs - frequent posting, direct address, self-disclosure, consistent authenticity
sources.citation: Witzel, L. D. The Cultivation and Harvesting of Parasocial Relationships for Evangelism: An Exploratory Multiple Case Study of Pastors' Use of Video on Social Media (Liberty University doctoral dissertation).

sources.claim: And the one technique conspicuously MISSING: expressing positive feelings. The emotional register the secular apparatus requires most is the one the priests dropped, and the harvest step changed accordingly - secular influencers monetize, priests direct people into a spiritual journey
sources.citation: Witzel, The Cultivation and Harvesting of Parasocial Relationships for Evangelism.

sources.claim: The field's own velocity, for scale: papers on parasocial experience grew fourfold between 2013 and 2020, with over 400 peer-reviewed papers and dissertations published in 2024 alone
sources.citation: Witzel, citing Liebers & Schramm (2023) and Forster, The Oxford Handbook of Parasocial Experiences (2023).

entries.title: Margery Kempe
entries.summary: English woman who experienced what she described as an unbreakable bond with Jesus, was mocked for weeping in church, was reviled by her family, and in 1438 dictated a book about it that persuaded other women to do the same.
entries.significance: The single strongest real case in the catalogue, and it is eight hundred years early. A bond with a figure who never appears in the physical world. A text as the medium. Grief when the access was withdrawn, which is the Replika update. And a recruitment function: the book exists to make other women feel what she felt, which is what a parasocial relationship is for.

sources.claim: Kempe dictated The Book of My First Showings c.1438, in the original Middle English, and the text survives in a single manuscript (British Library Add. 39903). She dictated it to scribes because she could not write.
sources.citation: Kempe, Margaret (ed. Frances E. Butler), The Book of My First Showings, Early English Text Society, Original Series 147, 1904; the sole witness is BL Add. 39903, transcribed in the 1904 EETS edition.

sources.claim: She was imprisoned in 1415-1416 largely over this writing and its reception.
sources.citation: Kempe's later accounts name imprisonment by the Bishop of London; the 1438 text is conventionally read against it.

entries.title: Binding
entries.summary: Performing a self until the self holds, where it can be witnessed. Margery Kempe in white clothes in a world where widows wore black, weeping loudly in public for years, having decided she was going to be a specific kind of person.
entries.significance: The founding document. It has three ingredients - a public, a performance, and witnesses who disapprove - and every parasocial dynamic since has those three. The neighbours thought she was unwell. The only thing that has changed is what the audience thinks about the person who is unwell.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Kempe, M. The Book of Margery Kempe

entries.title: The Book of My First Showings
entries.summary: A short prose book dictated by Margery Kempe describing her experiences of Christ's love, her suffering, and her certainty that she had been chosen.
entries.significance: The first person in this catalogue to write the thing down and then hand the book to other people. That second half is the part that makes it parasocial rather than merely devotional: the text is an instrument for producing the bond in somebody else.

sources.claim: Composed c.1438, surviving in one manuscript.
sources.citation: See the EETS edition cited under margery-kempe.

entries.title: Miguel de Cervantes
entries.summary: Author of Don Quixote, and of a narrator who keeps having to explain away the reality of what his character is doing.
entries.significance: Wrote the book in which the gap between a fictional world and a real one is argued out loud, by the person best placed to know.

sources.claim: Author; the two parts were published 1605 and 1615.
sources.citation: Standard bibliographic record.

entries.title: The audience
entries.summary: A room of people responding to a performance, learning the timing of the person on the stage.
entries.significance: Theatre invented the responsestream, and the performer learns to read it. Two thousand years before a chat log, the same feedback loop with worse latency and a room.

entries.title: Don Quixote
entries.summary: An old man who reads so many books about chivalry that he goes out to live as a knight, against all evidence.
entries.significance: The founding case of a reader who mistakes a book for a world and then lives in it anyway. The whole book's plot is the argument that a person can be entirely sincere about a bond with something that is not there, and the reader is not asked to think less of him for it.

sources.claim: Cervantes, Don Quixote, part one 1605, part two 1615.
sources.citation: Cervantes Saavedra, Miguel de, Don Quixote, 1605 and 1615.

entries.title: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
entries.summary: Author of Werther, and of the observation that people keep making the same mistakes, which is arguably the first great novel to describe a reader being changed by a book.
entries.significance: Wrote the most influential suicide in European literature and then spent his life doing the opposite of his character.

sources.claim: Author of Werther (1774) and of the Elective Affinities (1809).
sources.citation: Standard biographical record.

entries.title: Werther
entries.summary: The young man of Goethe's novel who reads too much, loves a woman who does not love him back, and kills himself, in a book that made that behaviour fashionable across Europe for a decade.
entries.significance: The prototype of the reader who goes looking for a character in order to feel something, and then brings the feeling home. Published in 1774; within two years the resulting condition had a name, Wertherfieber, and ministers of religion were issuing warnings about it.

sources.claim: Goethe, The Sorrows of Young Werther, 1774; the Werther fever it provoked is documented in the reception history of the period.
sources.citation: Goethe, J. W. von, Die Leiden des jungen Werthers, 1774; reception documented in the standard accounts of European sensibility.

entries.title: Charles Dickens
entries.summary: Serialised fiction to a mass audience, weekly, to people who could not afford a book but could not afford not to read it.
entries.significance: Built the first audience for fiction that was reliably weekly, enormous, and not present in the room.

sources.claim: Novelist and serial publisher; dates standard.
sources.citation: Standard biographical record.

entries.title: Miss Havisham
entries.summary: A woman in Great Expectations who is left jilted at the altar, stops eating, ages, and arranges to be found the way she was on her wedding day - decades later, in a wedding dress, in a darkened room.
entries.significance: The most complete fictional treatment of the object of a parasocial bond being a person who was never real, and of the grief outliving the reasons for it. She is not a metaphor for a fictional character, she is a person who has mistaken her own wedding for a plot.

sources.claim: Dickens, Great Expectations, 1861, Book 1, chapter 8 and chapter 19.
sources.citation: Dickens, Charles, Great Expectations, 1861.

entries.title: Identification with a team
entries.summary: Supporting a club as a condition of belonging to a place, a class, a family, or a city.
entries.significance: A parasocial bond with an address. The team is the only large-scale attachment in modern life that arrives with geography attached, which is why a relegation is felt as a personal event by people who have never met the players.

sources.claim: The mechanism, fifty years before anyone wrote about parasocial relationships: identification with a group is itself a source of self-esteem, and people derive it from membership rather than from any property of the team
sources.citation: Tajfel, H., & Turner, J. C. (1979). An integrative theory of intergroup conflict.

entries.title: The trading stamp
entries.summary: A loyalty scheme by paper coupon, redeemable at any participating shop, popular decades before loyalty cards existed.
entries.significance: The first loyalty scheme, and it is already the whole modern mechanism: a discount in exchange for the customer choosing this shop repeatedly. The paper only changed.

sources.claim: A peer-reviewed history of the mechanism in the United States, covering 1891-2008. The title's own span is what dates the entry: the documented run of trading stamps begins in 1891, not the decade earlier this entry previously claimed.
sources.citation: Elnahla, N., & Neilson, L. C. Getting something for nothing: the history of trading stamps in the United States of America (1891-2008).

sources.claim: Schuster's Department Store, Milwaukee issued the first stamps in 1890-91, specifically to push cash customers away from credit; L.H. Parke followed in 1895; S&H Green Stamps launched 1896, first customer a housewife in a Jackson, Michigan dry goods store
sources.citation: Something for everyone? The rise and fall of trading stamps (2024), drawing on the Hartman Center archives, Duke University.

sources.claim: Scale: in the 1950s-60s S&H printed three times as many stamps as the US Post Office, and its 1964 catalogue was the largest single publication in the United States. Andy Warhol painted the stamps
sources.citation: Trading Stamps. Encyclopedia.com.

sources.claim: The retailer case, with USDA field studies: sustained sales lift, and S&H claiming a 15-20% increase was needed to make stamps pay
sources.citation: Johnson, C. K. Trading stamps and the retailer. (USDA Marketing Division studies).

sources.claim: The trading economy persists in its modern form: fan forums are used for buying, selling and TRADING photocards
sources.citation: Ascue et al., Annyeong, Saranghae (De La Salle University).

entries.title: The comic strip
entries.summary: A recurring cast of characters, in a fixed panel order, appearing every single day without exception for decades.
entries.significance: The first daily serial in print and the template for the daily TV schedule that followed it. Continuity is the mechanism: you come back because yesterday happened to them too.

sources.claim: The newspaper strip was the first mass parasocial apparatus: a recurring, scheduled, addressed-to-everyone relationship delivered daily to a reader who never had to identify themselves to receive it
sources.citation: Comic strip (Wikipedia).

entries.title: Alfred Hitchcock
entries.summary: Director who said he made films about the tension between a man and the thing he cannot have.
entries.significance: Stated the thesis of this whole site, in his own words, before the word parasocial existed.

sources.claim: Statements in interview about suspense being the withholding of information, and about Vertigo's protagonist.
sources.citation: Hitchcock on Hitchcock, ed. François Truffaut, 1966 - the Vertigo chapter covers this directly.

entries.title: The coach
entries.summary: An adult with authority over a child for years, who is remembered partly by how they made them feel at nine.
entries.significance: The entry used to claim nobody had asked about this, and that was wrong in the specific way this site keeps getting things wrong: the coach-athlete relationship is one of the most-studied relationships in developmental psychology, and 'positive and sustained adult-youth relations' is one of the characteristics most strongly associated with the outcomes. What has never been examined is the shape of it. The bond is scored as an outcome - connection is one of the four things a coach is judged on producing - and never described as what it structurally is: an adult holding authority over a child who cannot leave, for years, and who is then remembered long after the authority has gone. That is a parasocial arrangement with a power gradient in it, and the field studying it has no word for that. The site does not yet have the evidence either.

sources.citation: Holt, N. L., Neely, K. C., Slater, L. G., Camire, M., Cote, J., Fraser-Thomas, J., MacDonald, D., Strachan, L., & Tamminen, K. A. (2017). A grounded theory of positive youth development through sport based on results from a qualitative meta-study. International Review of Sport and Exercise Psychology, 10(1), 1-49. (First published online 4 September 2016.)
sources.claim: A meta-synthesis of 63 qualitative studies, and the direct refutation of this entry's claim that nobody has asked about the coach. One of its three emergent categories is the 'PYD climate' - adult relationships, peer relationships and parental involvement. It reports that 'positive and sustained adult-youth relations' is one of the Big 3 programme characteristics associated with development; that Cote, Turnidge & Evans' Personal Assets Framework places 'relational factors (i.e., quality relationships)' among its three elements, generating change in confidence, competence, connection and character when repeated over time; and that Catalano et al. list 'warm, supportive relationships' among eight programme characteristics. Open access, CC BY-NC-ND.

sources.citation: Cote, J., & Gilbert, W. (2009). An Integrative Definition of Coaching Effectiveness and Expertise. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching, 4(3), 307-323.
sources.claim: The source of the 4 Cs that coaching effectiveness is measured against: competence, confidence, connection and character. Connection is defined as 'positive bonds and social relationships with people inside and outside of sport' - so the relational bond is one of the four things a coach is explicitly judged on producing. Volume and issue confirmed against Crossref as 4(3); the journal's own landing page says 4(4), and Crossref was preferred. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request.

entries.title: The landlord
entries.summary: A named individual with access to your home, your deposits and your address, met in person, repeatedly, under stress.
entries.significance: A parasocial relationship with somebody who holds a key and a legal claim, and the only entry on this site where the two are the same person rather than a system. Section 07 exists because the feeling and the power are inversely related, which is the definition of the problem. The housing literature has actually found the mechanism, without using this site's vocabulary: renters describe landlords warmly, and then decline to raise legitimate complaints because escalating might damage the relationship - including in the cases they describe as positive. What keeps a bad tenancy in place is not the lease and not the law but the prospect of the next landlord being worse, which is an attachment to a named individual, formed under stress, with no way to leave without losing the address.

sources.citation: Byrne, M., & McArdle, R. (2020). Secure occupancy, power and the landlord-tenant relation: a qualitative exploration of the Irish private rental sector. Housing Studies, 37(1), 124-142.
sources.claim: States the relationship in the terms this entry has been arguing for: tenant and landlord are 'not merely equal parties to a contract, nor are they atomised market actors. They are tied together in a relationship which is both a social relationship and a power relationship' (quoted at p. 139 in McKee & Harris below). A social relationship and a power relationship in the same clause is the whole problem, and it is in the abstract of record for the subject. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request; volume, issue and pages confirmed against Crossref.

sources.citation: McKee, K., & Harris, J. (2023). The role of landlords in shaping private renters' uneven experiences of home: towards a relational approach. International Journal of Housing Policy, 25(1), 101-118.
sources.claim: Documents the mechanism this entry asserts. Renter interviews: tenants praised landlords who communicated well and were responsive, and yet, on further probing, 'some tenants simply did not want to raise legitimate issues or escalate complaints where issues remained unaddressed because of the risk of damaging the relationship with their landlord' - which the authors note persisted even where the relationship was described positively. The 'imagined alternative' of a negative relationship in the next tenancy was the powerful driver for accepting the status quo. A tenant staying silent to protect a relationship with someone who holds the keys and the deposit is a one-sided attachment, described here entirely in the language of housing policy. Publisher returns 403.

sources.citation: Soaita, A. M. (2024). The social vibe of the tenant/landlord relationship in a 'tenant market': the case of Romania. Housing Studies, 40(11), 2428-2449.
sources.claim: Frames the gap this entry sits in: while interest in private rental housing has grown, 'few studies have addressed the tenant/landlord relationship as lived' - as a relationship rather than a contract. Examines narratives of risk and the repertoires of risk mitigation that renters build. Publisher returns 403; bibliographic record confirmed against Crossref.

entries.title: The teacher
entries.summary: An authority figure seen daily, for years, who knows your name, your mood and your home situation.
entries.significance: The parasocial bond nobody writes about because the power is unequal and the field has spent fifty years on the unequal-power case while leaving this one alone.

sources.claim: Measured in a classroom, n=248 junior high students: parasocial interaction with an instructor has a SIGNIFICANT POSITIVE impact on motivational interest (beta=.624, p<.005), which in turn reduces extraneous cognitive load
sources.citation: Liu, X., & Li, C. (2024). The Effects of Social Cues in Self-Produced Micro Video Lectures on Parasocial Interaction, Motivational Interest, Extraneous Cognitive Load, and Concept Learning Performance.

sources.claim: And the honest null in the same paper: adding MORE types of social cue made no measurable difference across four groups. Warmth is not a dial you can simply turn up

A second honest null, from educational YouTube: no correlation between parasocial interaction and actual LEARNING GROWTH, though a slight correlation with motivation, stronger for female participants. The bond changes how hard people try, not what they retain
sources.citation: Beautemps, J., & Bresges, A. (2022). The influence of the parasocial relationship on the learning motivation and learning growth with educational YouTube videos in self regulated learning.

entries.title: The transfer
entries.summary: A player who has been attached to for years leaves, and the grievance is felt as betrayal by the entire locality.
entries.significance: The standard parasocial grievance story, and the one nobody frames as parasocial. The word for the feeling is betrayal, which is a relationship word, applied to a person who never signed anything - and the research says that is not sentiment, it is structure. Fans identify more strongly with the club than with any individual who plays for it, identification transfers between the two, and it survives the pairing being dissolved. Which is why the departing player absorbs an attachment that was never really his. Both sides also treat the transfer as carrying a real obligation: players talk about a pledge to supporters that appears in no contract, which is the whole trouble with a relationship word applied to a commercial transaction.

sources.citation: Merten, S., Reuland, N., Winand, M., & Marlier, M. (2020). Fan identification in football: professional football players and clubs competing for fan loyalty. Sport, Business and Management: An International Journal, 14(2), 169-187.
sources.claim: The mechanism, and it runs opposite to the usual account. Measured with a fan identification scale: fans identify MORE strongly with their favourite team than with their favourite individual player, and connection to a player is weaker if he never played for that team. Identification therefore transfers between team and player and remains 'long-lasting, even after the combination of both actors has been dissolved' - compared in the paper to research on supporters of relocated clubs. So the grievance lands on the departing individual because the durable attachment is to the club. Publisher returns 403; Crossref-confirmed.

sources.citation: Herd, K. (2023). Transfer patterns in the Swedish football clubs - a gift economy of loyalties and emotions. Soccer & Society, 25(3), 257-271.
sources.claim: Interview study in which players and fans treat a transfer as simultaneously an investment, a step in a career and 'a pledge to supporters' - players describing real obligations and expectations of supporters, and supporters describing attachment to players. The pledge is understood as binding by both sides and documented in no contract, which is what makes the word 'betrayal' available. Concludes that the market may be described as an emotional economy in which money is a means rather than a goal. Publisher returns 403.

sources.citation: Kaden, M., Brandt, C., Bauers, S. B., Bunar, J., & Hovemann, G. (2023). "I don't watch that anymore": an analysis of online comments by German soccer fans on their relationship to their favored clubs. Frontiers in Psychology, 14.
sources.claim: The other side of the same bond: supporters' exits, analysed through Hirschman's exit-voice-loyalty framework. Finds German soccer fans inclined to voice rather than exit, but with demonstrable limits - some supporting a non-league club instead - and quotes the finding that consumption of professional soccer 'cannot be ceased altogether'. Notes the commercialisation critique that players are transferred 'like assets' without regard to the local fan community, producing alienation between players and fans. Open access.

sources.citation: Fillis, I., & Mackay, C. (2014). Moving beyond fan typologies: the impact of social integration on team loyalty in football. Journal of Marketing Management, 30(3-4), 334-363.
sources.claim: Moves past tiered fan typologies to argue that devotion is best explained through social integration and a religious frame - religiosity and sacred consumption accounting for committed supporters of a single club, who see themselves as members of it and are unlikely to transfer allegiance. Case study of a Scottish club and its supporters. Author accepted manuscript in the University of Stirling repository.

entries.title: The film serial
entries.summary: Episodes released in instalments, each ending unresolved, the audience expected to return for the next one.
entries.significance: The cliffhanger as an industrial practice rather than a narrative trick, and the direct ancestor of the soap and the serialised novel.

sources.claim: American serials begin in 1912 as publisher-sponsored film adaptations of their own magazine characters, to build interest and boost circulation - the parasocial mechanism, documented, at the start of cinema
sources.citation: Serial film. Wikipedia, citing trade histories. Serials in the United States first came about in 1912 as extensions of magazine and newspaper stories; publishers sponsored live-action adventures of the printed characters to boost circulation.

sources.claim: The first serial: What Happened to Mary (1912), Edison, 12 reels, Mary Fuller, released one chapter per month alongside the story in McClure's Ladies' World from 26 July 1912
sources.citation: Serial Films: Part 1. filmsite.org.

sources.claim: The early audience was female - thrills rather than blood-and-thunder - and the format ran to 1956
sources.citation: EBSCO Research Starters, Film Serials.

entries.title: Green Shield Stamps
entries.summary: A national loyalty scheme in Britain, redeemed for goods, with a book of stamps kept in the house.
entries.significance: The first loyalty programme most families would have lived with for a generation, and a physical object in the home. The customer's book of stamps is an account balance that lives in a cupboard, which is a genius piece of interface design that nobody has beaten.

sources.claim: Launched in the United Kingdom in 1958, Green Shield Stamps is among the longest-running trading-stamp loyalty schemes and remains in circulation decades later. The card outlived most of the shops that issued it
sources.citation: Green Shield Stamps (Wikipedia).

entries.title: The fan mail department
entries.summary: A physical object that had to be opened, a volume small enough for one person to hold, and a reply that was an exception. Clara Bow, Shirley Temple, Judy Garland, all had staff whose job was correspondence. Some of it came back.
entries.significance: The relationship before the technology that supposedly caused it. What the mail got right is rhythm and scarcity: it arrived, it was opened, sometimes it was answered. What the internet removed was the reply and the rhythm, not the feeling. Every 'the internet invented parasocial relationships' argument collapses here.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its sources added.

entries.title: The athlete and the city
entries.summary: Support for a team or an athlete as a bond with a person, a place and a lineage, frequently inherited from a parent.
entries.significance: The most durable parasocial bond in the world and the one least discussed as parasocial, because it is assumed to be about sport. The transfer window is the standard betrayal story, which is a parasocial grievance wearing a football shirt.

sources.claim: 'Fan' entered English usage for baseball spectators in the eighteenth century - the athlete-and-city bond predates the film star by a century
sources.citation: Fan Culture. EBSCO Research Starters, Social Sciences and Humanities.

entries.title: The first fans
entries.summary: The first documented fan clubs, organised around sheet music and radio rather than film. Following became joining.
entries.significance: The behaviour did not arrive with any technology. It arrived with the possibility of being heard, and a great deal of organisation, done unpaid, by people who were young.

sources.claim: Verified, not assumed: 1920-30-40 US census records were used to establish which letters in Picture Play's fan-mail pages were written by real, existing fans - so the first fandom is documented as actual people, not as a later projection
sources.citation: Lanckman, L. (2020). Fans, community, and conflict in the pages of 'Picture Play'. Transformative Works and Culture.

sources.claim: THE CONDUIT, DEFINED BY SUPPLY FAILURE. Clara Bow's fans asked her fan magazine what colour her hair and eyes were - in a black-and-white medium. The magazine supplied what the film could not. Henna sales tripled because her hair was red
sources.citation: Gordon, M. Making It in Hollywood: Clara Bow, Fandom, and Consumer Culture.

sources.claim: Scale of the first fandom: 45,000 fan letters a week to Clara Bow at her 1929 peak, and 500,000 circulation fan magazines at 5-25 cents
sources.citation: Gordon, M. Making It in Hollywood: Clara Bow, Fandom, and Consumer Culture, citing Stenn, Clara Bow Runnin' Wild (1988) and St. Johns, Love, Laughter, and Tears (1978).

entries.title: The cliffhanger
entries.summary: End the episode before the answer. Give the viewer a fixed slot, a daily rhythm, and a question with no resolution, and they will come back tomorrow at the same time for years.
entries.significance: The oldest engagement mechanic in media and the most efficient. A cliffhanger is not a plot device, it is a scheduling device - it converts a feeling into a diary entry. A twelve-part serial is not a story, it is a habit with characters in it.

sources.claim: The scholarly account of seriality as structure rather than trick: Mittell's complex TV argues the modern serial builds meaning through accumulated paratext, discussion and anticipation across time rather than within the episode
sources.citation: Mittell, J. (2015). Complex TV: The Poetics of Contemporary Television Storytelling.

sources.claim: And the experimental result: 44 children assigned to serial or episodic delivery of the same story engaged more persistently with the serial
sources.citation: To Pause With a Cliffhanger or a Temporary Closure: Serial vs. episodic narratives and sustained engagement.

entries.title: Radio and the soap
entries.summary: Broadcast drama on a fixed daily slot, written for an audience with nowhere else to be at that hour.
entries.significance: The audience and the medium are the same thing. A radio serial is a routine, and the routine is the relationship.

sources.claim: Fan mail as perceived interactivity in the 1920s-30s: listeners experienced two-way communication through letters even though radio had no interactive technology. The conclusion - that interactivity may depend on media content rather than media technology - is this site's thesis, in 2009
sources.citation: Simmons, C. (2009). Dear Radio Broadcaster: Fan Mail as a Form of Perceived Interactivity.

sources.claim: The finding that fans negotiated and policed their own codes of behaviour in fan magazines - a community regulating itself without a platform
sources.citation: Lanckman, L. (2020). Fans, community, and conflict in the pages of 'Picture Play'. Transformative Works and Culture.

entries.title: The soap opera
entries.summary: A form built almost entirely by women, for women, and treated as unserious for fifty years. Daily episodes, fixed slots, cliffhangers, characters written in indefinitely and never resolved.
entries.significance: The origin of the entire research tradition, and it started as a footnote about daytime television that nobody thought was important. The rhythm is the mechanism: a fixed slot and an unresolved story, repeated daily, is a relationship with a schedule. It is also the reason the phrase 'soap opera' is now an insult rather than a description.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Schlesinger, P. (1932, 1933), WGN

entries.title: The first superhero
entries.summary: A character who cannot die, printed in a newspaper, read by a generation of children on the same day.
entries.significance: The first parasocial figure with an explicit immortality guarantee, which is the trade being made: I will never get over this, and I will never have to find out. Nobody has ever been made this offer in a relationship.

sources.claim: Superman's first comic-book appearance was 1938; newspapers in early 1939, radio February 1940
sources.citation: EBSCO Research Starters, Film Serials (chronology of the character's media appearances).

sources.claim: Republic Pictures negotiated with Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster for a serial, and went to another hero when they demanded script control - creators versus commercial terms, early
sources.citation: EBSCO Research Starters, Film Serials.

sources.claim: The genre that made the character worked on television, not film: Columbia's 1948 Superman used cartoon animation for flight because effects were unaffordable
sources.citation: Film International, 'A World of Constant Peril: Seriality, Narrative and Closure' (2014).

entries.title: The protagonist is a parasocial object
entries.summary: The first-person film, the subjective shot, the character who exists to be looked through rather than at.
entries.significance: A technical innovation that produced a psychological one. Putting the camera inside somebody's eyes makes the audience's position structurally identical to the character's, which is the whole friendship with a film in one device.

entries.title: The bobby-soxers
entries.summary: Teenagers organised in public, in letterpress newsletters, to buy records and argue about a singer. A press of ten thousand.
entries.significance: The first parasocial mass movement with its own publishing, its own jargon and its own antagonism toward the parents of the people in it. Everything since is a re-skin.

sources.claim: The teenage 'bobby-soxer', a term from the 1940s, and the scream that made one - the press turned a sound at a Sinatra performance into a generational diagnosis of mass hysteria. The first recorded audience parasocial event
sources.citation: Bobby-soxer (Wikipedia).

entries.title: Wishful thinking
entries.summary: The long-standing explanation that parasocial feeling is a projection - people attach to a figure because the figure is available to be shaped by whoever is looking.
entries.significance: Still the most intuitive theory and the least satisfying one, because it makes the relationship entirely internal to the viewer. The research moved away from it, not because projection is wrong, but because it cannot explain why a specific figure reaches a specific person and nobody else does.

entries.title: Gigi
entries.summary: The song where the singer pleads to be given the exact shape a man wants: a French phrase, a café in the dark. A whole musical built around wanting to be a specific imaginary person for somebody.
entries.significance: The template for a large fraction of the twentieth century. Cole Porter did not invent the impulse, he published it, and the song is still the most precise description of the thing that every subsequent song about obsessive attachment is a worse version of.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Porter, C. (1943). 'Gigi'.

entries.title: Nick Drake
entries.summary: Made three records, withdrew from touring, and left behind an audience that argues about what he meant for fifty years.
entries.significance: The clearest case of the bond forming after the person withdrew from it, and of the work becoming the only place the relationship could continue.

sources.claim: Three studio albums, 1968-1974; withdrew from live performance 1969-70.
sources.citation: Standard discographic record.

entries.title: The fan club
entries.summary: A formal organisation with membership, dues, an elected president, a newsletter and rules. Not a spontaneous thing that happened to fans - a structure somebody built for them and that fans then ran themselves.
entries.significance: The first institutional form, and the origin of nearly everything downstream including the paid tiers. The important part is that fans built a lot of it themselves, which is the strongest evidence that the impulse is real and the structure is optional.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its sources added.

entries.title: Gazing at celebrities
entries.summary: The early frames on attraction to media figures, work that treated the person doing the gazing as a slightly odd specimen and the celebrity as an object of study rather than a participant.
entries.significance: Historians use it as a mark of how far the field has moved. Almost nothing in the current literature treats the viewer as strange. The interesting correction is not that gazing is normal but that the frame itself was the problem - one person studied, the other one an object.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its sources added.

entries.title: The retail clerk
entries.summary: A person who recognises you, remembers what you wanted, and has the right thing behind the counter when you come back.
entries.significance: The origin of the site mascot and the most parasocial job in retail, which nobody has ever written a paper about. It is also the most useful control condition: the same attention, delivered by a person who gets paid to give it.

entries.title: The local news anchor
entries.summary: One person on your own television, in your own town, for twenty years, who is leaving and everybody is upset.
entries.significance: Rubin's longitudinal work is on exactly this bond. When a local anchor retires the grief is measurable and there is no word for it, because a parasocial relationship with a local figure is assumed to be about the news rather than about the person.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Rubin et al., 1985

entries.title: The neighbour
entries.summary: Someone whose kitchen light you can see, whose bin day you know, and whose life you have been tracking for years without ever having asked.
entries.significance: A parasocial bond with somebody who is physically present and therefore, apparently, cannot be the subject of one. The reasoning is that proximity disqualifies attachment, which is exactly backwards and is why Section 07 was empty for so long.

sources.claim: The canonical account of why proximity without contact produces a relationship at all: weak ties carry information and feelings that strong ties cannot, and the value of an acquaintance is precisely that it is un-demanded
sources.citation: Granovetter, M. S. (1973). The Strength of Weak Ties. American Journal of Sociology, 78(6), 1360-1380.

sources.claim: The city's price for that: the essay tradition on urban indifference describes exactly the condition this entry describes - you can know a person's habits from their kitchen light without ever having been introduced, and the arrangement suits both parties
sources.citation: Sennett, R. The Conscience of the Eye: The Architecture and Morality of Public Space.

entries.title: The Macy's counter
entries.summary: A sales clerk who remembered. Not a recommendation engine, not a loyalty points balance - a person who noticed what you had looked at and had the right thing ready when you came back.
entries.significance: The historical control condition. Every 'personalised' retail system since is an attempt to reproduce what one person could do for a few hundred regulars, and none of them have done it as well, because the thing that made it work was not the data. It was that it was somebody's job to pay attention.

entries.title: Elvis Presley
entries.summary: A national simultaneous viewing event, and an industry that learned within two years that the appeal was not the music.
entries.significance: The founding demonstration that a parasocial bond can be manufactured deliberately, at scale, for commercial return. The Colonel Tom Parker apparatus is the first parasocial persuasion machine.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: The Colonel Parker apparatus

entries.title: Parasocial interaction
entries.summary: The name itself. Coined to describe the way viewers responded to a television character they followed consistently - a bond with somebody who did not know they existed. Parasocial: one-sided, parallel to the para- in paranormal.
entries.significance: The coinage is defensive and that is the story. It was invented in the McCarthy era to describe a television habit that was considered slightly shameful - viewers writing in about soap characters as though they could be defamed. The word bakes in an apology for the feeling. The feeling did not need one.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Horton, D., & Wohl, R. R. (1956). Mass communication and para-social interaction: Observations on intimacy at a distance. Psychiatry, 19(3), 215-229.

sources.claim: THE FOUNDING CITATION for the term this entire site runs on, coined in 1956 for psychological attachment to television personalities, and quoted for the 'exchange' at p.218
sources.citation: Horton, D., & Wohl, R. R. (1956). Mass Communication and Social Interaction: Observations on Intimacy at a Distance. Psychiatry, 19(3), 215-229.

entries.title: Vertigo
entries.summary: A man is asked to follow a woman he can see but not touch, and is eventually given permission to do exactly that.
entries.significance: The most constructed version of the one-sided bond ever filmed, and a film about the person doing the constructing rather than the person being constructed. Hitchcock understood that the object was never the point.

sources.claim: Hitchcock, Alfred, dir., Vertigo, 1958, Paramount.
sources.citation: Standard filmographic record.

entries.title: The manufactured teen idol
entries.summary: A television family show repurposed as a launchpad: the first rock-and-roll teen idol was on screen from birth, and his parents edited his episodes into the earliest music videos. Assembled, yes - by television.
entries.significance: The first documented case of an attachment being designed as a manufacturing process, and the supply chain ran through television rather than through a label - which is this site's argument arriving eighty years early. Rick Nelson was a character in his parents' weekly sitcom from birth, and the series was then used to sell records: he was the first teen idol to promote hit records on television, and his father had the idea of cutting episode footage into music videos. The attachment came first and the product was attached to it, which is the reverse of the usual story about a star being promoted. One caveat on the entry's own vocabulary: the practice is early 1950s, but the word is later - Nelson's 1962 record helped universalise 'teen idol', so the term names the phenomenon a few years after the thing existed. That lag is itself the pattern: the bond is always there before anyone has words for it.

sources.citation: Ricky Nelson. Wikipedia.
sources.claim: The manufacturing plant was a television family show, not a record label: 'Nelson was the first teen idol to use television to promote hit records. Ozzie Nelson even had the idea to edit footage together to create some of the first music videos', the edit being visible in the video for 'Travelin' Man'. He had been a screen presence since birth playing himself in his parents' weekly series, which is the whole supply chain: the attachment preceded the product and was then monetised through it.

sources.citation: Ricky Nelson. EBSCO Research Starters (History).
sources.claim: Called 'the first rock-and-roll teen idol', and Nelson parlayed his visibility in the weekly sitcom into a pop career - which is the entry's claim, sourced. Also dates the vocabulary: his 1962 hit 'Teenage Idol' helped universalise the term, so the phrase postdates the practice by several years. Notes the contemporary fan-orientated paperback that captured the phenomenon as it happened, and cites Joel Selvin, Ricky Nelson: Idol for a Generation (Contemporary Books, 1990).

entries.title: The sitcom family
entries.summary: A recurring family, played by the same cast, five nights a week, for years, in a house you could draw from memory.
entries.significance: Attachment to a fictional household, watched nightly, in the pre-internet equivalent of a comfort rewatch. Research on sitcom parasocial attachment found the same pattern as soaps: it is the accumulation, not the plot.

sources.claim: N=840: appreciation and enjoyment are separate responses. Appreciation is being moved; enjoyment is pleasure. Tragic outcomes still produce appreciation even where enjoyment is absent - the family you miss was never the fun one
sources.citation: Krakowiak, K. M. (2024). How It Ends: Exploring How Narrative Closure and Character Outcomes in Series Finales Relate to Viewer Responses and Coping Behaviors.

sources.claim: And the mechanism that makes loss social: appreciation INCREASED coping behaviours - seeking more information, reading analyses, discussing with other viewers - while enjoyment decreased them. Feeling moved makes you go and talk to someone
sources.citation: Krakowiak, K. M. (2024). How It Ends.

entries.title: The political parasocial
entries.summary: Support for a politician structured as a personal bond rather than a policy preference, in a way that transfers poorly across candidates.
entries.significance: The oldest public parasocial bond is the sovereign, and it is the one the field has consistently declined to study. A stadium and a parliament are the same room with different seating plans.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Spectator Australia, 2026

entries.title: Dionne Warwick's fan mail
entries.summary: She received correspondence by the sackful and answered it by name, individually, for years. The closest thing the twentieth century produced to a genuinely reciprocal parasocial relationship.
entries.significance: The proof that reciprocity is possible and therefore a choice, not a law of nature. Every subsequent complaint that the parasocial relationship has no reply is answering a question she had already settled.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Warwick, D. (1994). Memories of a lifetime.

entries.title: Beatlesmania
entries.summary: A global mass hysteria, documented live, with screaming, fainting, and an industry that began pricing it within months.
entries.significance: The first time the world watched itself develop a parasocial disorder in real time, and the first time anybody seriously proposed monetising it. The licensing of merchandising set the template for everything since.

sources.claim: THE FIRST FAN BEHAVIOUR MEASURED RATHER THAN DIAGNOSED. 346 subjects aged 15-20, tested shortly after the Beatles' Wellington visit, split into 50 keenest, 122 moderate, 50 'resisters'. The authors found NO evidence on the MMPI Hysteria Scale and no supporting clinical evidence of neuroticism, and teachers reported none needed referral
sources.citation: Taylor, A. J. W. (1966). Beatlemania - A Study in Adolescent Enthusiasm. British Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, 5(2), 81-88.

sources.claim: Their conclusion, quoted in the abstract: Beatlemania is 'the passing reaction of predominantly young adolescent females to group pressures of such a kind that meet their special emotional needs.' Developmentally real, not clinically
sources.citation: Taylor, A. J. W. (1966). Beatlemania - A Study in Adolescent Enthusiasm.

sources.claim: What the fans said the apparatus was. First-generation fan Candy Leonard, now a scholar of it: 'the mags were a way to extend/enhance the experience... We saw the Beatles as extended family and that was the way to keep up with them. The records, the transistor radio, the merch, the conversation, and the magazines created what I call a wraparound experience'
sources.citation: Bumsted, A. 1960s Teen Fan Magazines and The Beatles, interviews with first-generation fan Candy Leonard.

sources.claim: The turn, dated by a fan to a record: Leonard places the change at Rubber Soul (December 1965), the moment 'the Beatles came to occupy a role in fans' lives and a place in their psyches that was different from any previous fan-performer relationship'
sources.citation: Candy Leonard, Beatleness: George Beatles and the Beatles' Legacy (2014).

sources.claim: The hostile framing, for the ledger: Paul Johnson wrote in the New Statesman in February 1964 that the mania was a modern incarnation of female hysteria and that the fans at their concerts were 'the least fortunate of their generation, the dull, the idle, the failures'. It became the most complained-about piece in that magazine's history
sources.citation: Beatlemania (Wikipedia), citing Paul Johnson, New Statesman, February 1964.

sources.claim: The sympathetic reading, from the period: Ehrenreich, Hess and Jacobs argued Beatlemania was the first mass outburst of the sixties to feature women, girls who would not reach full adulthood until the seventies, and therefore 'the emergence of a genuinely political movement for women's liberation'
sources.citation: Ehrenreich, B., Hess, E., & Jacobs, G. (1986). Re-making Love: The Feminization of Sex.

sources.claim: And the reading that got there first: a 1997 study argued Beatlemania represented proto-feminist girl power, anticipating by thirty years what the archive would show
sources.citation: Beatlemania: A sexually defiant consumer subculture? (1997).

sources.claim: The band press officer's summary, offered as flattery and accurate anyway: Derek Taylor described the relationship between the Beatles and their fans as 'the twentieth century's greatest romance'
sources.citation: Beatlemania (Wikipedia), citing Derek Taylor.

entries.title: ELIZA
entries.summary: A short pattern-matching script that reflects the user's words back with questions attached. Most people told it they understood, within minutes.
entries.significance: The founding demonstration that an attentive-seeming system is enough, and that the belief is generated by the response rather than by the intelligence behind it. Every companion app since is a bigger ELIZA, and the field has still not fully absorbed what that first one proved.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Weizenbaum, 1966

entries.title: The dialogue programs
entries.summary: ELIZA, PARRY and Colby - three programs that convinced people they were listening.
entries.significance: All three were written to be good enough to be believed, and the belief was studied as a phenomenon rather than treated as a bug.

sources.claim: Weizenbaum (ELIZA), Colby (PARRY), and Colby's follow-up work.
sources.citation: Standard history of early natural-language programs, 1966-1975.

entries.title: Charisma as a measurable asset
entries.summary: Research on why some political candidates reliably produce personal attachment and others do not, despite comparable policy positions.
entries.significance: If charisma is a real and learnable thing, then attachment to public figures is manipulable by design, and the manipulation is not a side effect of the work.

sources.claim: The classical account of charisma as a political asset, and of its built-in instability: Weber's charismatic authority rests on devotion to the exceptional person rather than on rules or office, which is precisely why it cannot be institutionalised without being transformed
sources.citation: Weber, M. Economy and Society ( posthumous, 1922), on charismatic authority and its routinisation.

sources.claim: Weber's warning is the useful part for this site: charisma is understood to be unstable and to require routinisation into something impersonal, which is the same bargain described here from the other end
sources.citation: Weber, M. Economy and Society.

entries.title: Characters move in
entries.summary: The fictional thing rents space in someone's head and starts paying rent in meaning. You rehearse the encounters, you decorate them, you introduce them to friends like a roommate.
entries.significance: Fiction is the safest place on earth to find out what you actually feel, because nothing in there can disappoint you on purpose. The only line worth drawing is where the room starts making house rules - when the lore thread replaces the friend, or the edit replaces sleep. That line is always felt long before it can be explained.

sources.claim: A fictional character who moves into your home and stays: Mr. Belvedere, an English butler employed as a live-in housekeeper by an American family, 1985-1990, 117 episodes. He is nursemaid, cook, cleaner, confidant and conscience, and he never leaves until the finale
sources.citation: Mr. Belvedere (Wikipedia).

sources.claim: AND THE DEVICE THAT MAKES IT PARASOCIAL RATHER THAN SITCOM: every episode ends with Belvedere writing in his journal, giving the moral and putting the week's events in perspective. The character keeps a diary about the family - and about the audience watching him keep it
sources.citation: Mr. Belvedere - Plot (IMDb).

sources.claim: The setting was fabricated wholesale: the producers had never visited Pittsburgh, worked from a promotional calendar, and shot no scenes there. The household is a set of rooms in a place that does not exist
sources.citation: Mr. Belvedere (Wikipedia), reporting Dungan and Stein.

sources.claim: And the exit, which is the point: in the two-part finale he marries and moves to Africa, leaving the family. The character that moved in eventually has to leave, and the audience is not consulted
sources.citation: Mr. Belvedere - Premise (Liquisearch).

sources.claim: THE MECHANISM, STATED PLAINLY BY SOMEONE MEASURING IT: stories and story characters provide interpersonal intimacy WITHOUT THE THREAT OF REJECTION. That is the whole reason a fictional figure can be safer than a person
sources.citation: Rain, M., & Mar, R. A. (2021). Adult attachment and engagement with fictional characters.

sources.claim: And it is conditional, which is the uncomfortable part: attachment anxiety and avoidance DIFFERENTIALLY predict character identification and parasocial interaction, and a high-powered pre-registered follow-up found attachment orientation predicts which characters people are drawn to. Some characters are wanted because they are unavailable
sources.citation: Rain & Mar (2021).

sources.claim: Sometimes you are not watching the character, you ARE it - and the literature distinguishes the two. A player-avatar relationship can be MONADIC, where the player identifies with the avatar to the point of being the same being, or DYADIC, where a separation makes it closer to a parasocial relationship. Same apparatus, opposite structure
sources.citation: Ferchaud, A. (2024). Identification and Parasocial Relationships With Video Game Characters. Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Communication.

sources.claim: What it takes linguistically, from interviews with MMO players: SELF-DIFFERENTIATION and ANTHROPOMORPHIZATION together suspend disbelief enough for the figure to be taken as a fully social agent. You have to make it different from you and also human, at the same time
sources.citation: Avatars are (sometimes) people too: Linguistic indicators of parasocial and social ties in player-avatar relationships. New Media & Society.

sources.claim: The bond once mistaken for pathology is ordinary attachment style: research on intimate television viewing shows people forming relationships parasocially and insecurely, and treats it as a predictable outcome of disposition rather than a malfunction
sources.citation: Cole, T., & Leets, L. (1999). Attachment Styles and Intimate Television Viewing: Insecurely Forming Relationships in a Parasocial Way. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 16(4), 495-511.

sources.claim: And the predictable ending, named in the literature: parasocial break-up from favourite television characters is studied as its own phenomenon, driven by attachment style and relationship intensity rather than by anything the character did
sources.citation: Cohen, J. (2004). Parasocial Break-Up from Favorite Television Characters: The Role of Attachment Styles and Relationship Intensity. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 21(2), 187-202.

sources.claim: THE ABSENT REPLY, WHICH IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT IN 1774. Werther writes to his friend Wilhelm but the reader never sees Wilhelm's replies - the letters are missing. The reader therefore becomes Wilhelm's stand-in and must supply the response themselves. An 18th-century readership expecting an explicit moral from the narrator is instead left to answer for a character who cannot answer
sources.citation: Goethe's Werther and its effects. The Lancet Psychiatry (2014).

sources.claim: But the epidemic is NOT established, and the site's honesty requires saying so: a systematic search of German, Austrian and Swiss newspaper databases since 1774 found eight previously undocumented suicides the press connected to the novel, while the papers themselves reported the 'Werther-epidemic' and its moral implications far more than individual imitative suicides. Whether it substantiates an epidemic remains up to interpretation
sources.citation: Anecdotal Evidence in Historical News Reports (2023), reviewing suicides the press connected to Goethe's Werther since 1774.

sources.claim: There is a counter-effect and it has a name too: the Papageno effect, after Mozart's character in The Magic Flute, in which portrayals of a character contemplating suicide who is prevented at the last moment reduce imitation. Media reporting guidelines exist for both. The mechanism runs in both directions and the site should not pretend otherwise
sources.citation: Goethe's Werther and its effects. The Lancet Psychiatry (2014), discussing the Werther and Papageno effects.

sources.claim: Byron called Goethe 'the first literary character in Europe' fifty years later, and Napoleon read the novel seven times before discussing it with its author in 1808
sources.citation: Goethe's Werther and its effects. The Lancet Psychiatry (2014), citing Bayard Quincy Morgan.

sources.claim: The register that this whole project is about, stated by the author: when he finished it Goethe likened his mood to being 'after a general confession, joyous and free and entitled to a new life'. For Goethe the Werther effect was cathartic. Not so for its readers
sources.citation: Goethe's Werther and its effects. The Lancet Psychiatry (2014), citing David Constantine's introduction to his translation.

entries.title: Grieving a person you never met
entries.summary: Collective mourning of a public figure, and the persistent argument about whether it counts. Measured in studies of soap opera finales finding grief markers the same shape as the end of a relationship.
entries.significance: The largest and most defensible category on this site. Losing somebody is what happens when the people you love die, and a very large number of people grieve in public and are told it is a symptom. The only unusual thing about parasocial grief is that the person could not have known you were there, and that deserves care rather than condescension.

sources.claim: Parasocial grief is real, measurable, and specifically disenfranchised: a death the world does not recognise as a loss
sources.citation: DeGroot, J. M., & Leith, A. P. (2018). R.I.P. Kutner: Parasocial Grief Following the Death of a Television Character. Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly, 77(3), 199-216.

sources.claim: Grief at the end of a long series, measured at scale (n=1289) after the Neighbours finale
sources.citation: Gerace, A. (2024). When TV neighbours become good friends: Understanding Neighbours fans' feelings of grief and loss at the end of the series. PLOS ONE.

sources.claim: Character death and series cancellation produce similar distress; voluntary withdrawal produces much less
sources.citation: Cuddy, L., & Ellithorpe, M. E. (2025). 'I was Absolutely Devastated at This Death': Refining the Conceptualization and Processes of Parasocial Breakup Distress.

sources.claim: Mourning is conducted on Facebook RIP pages for people the mourner never met
sources.citation: Klastrup, L. (2015). 'I didn't know her, but...': Parasocial mourning of mediated deaths on Facebook RIP pages. New Review of Hypermedia and Multimedia.

sources.claim: The framework's founding measurement of parasocial breakup
sources.citation: Eyal, K., & Cohen, J. (2006). When Good Friends Say Goodbye: A Parasocial Breakup Study. Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media, 50(3), 502-523.

sources.claim: Grief outcomes after a real celebrity death, and the role of parasocial relations in stigma and help-seeking
sources.citation: Hoffner, C. A., & Cohen, E. L. (2017). Mental Health-Related Outcomes of Robin Williams' Death. Health Communication, 33(12), 1573-1582.

sources.claim: THE CONTESTED CLAIM: relational closeness, not parasociality, predicts grief intensity at celebrity death - i.e. the grief is not the parasocial bond
sources.citation: Baker, A. C., & Cohen, E. L. (2023). Relational closeness - not parasociality - determines the intensity of grief responses to celebrity death. Death Studies, 48(8), 873-878.

entries.title: SHRDLU
entries.summary: A conversational system about a small blocks world, capable of genuinely tracking a user's intentions. Famous for one demonstration and a broken follow-up.
entries.significance: The proof that machine understanding of intent was considered a solved research problem in 1970 and has been failing privately ever since. The person who made SHRDLU then said the problem was far harder than it looked, and was believed by nobody.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Winograd, 1970

entries.title: The first convention
entries.summary: Fans gather, in costume, in a hotel ballroom, to be in the same room with people who feel the same way about a show.
entries.significance: The first mass physical assembly of parasocial people, and the proof that the bond had become a social fact requiring infrastructure. Everything after is logistics.

sources.claim: The first Star Trek convention, 3-5 March 1972 at the Hotel Commodore in New York, organised largely by James Doohan and his wife, drew a crowd far larger than the organisers had expected and is the direct ancestor of the modern comics convention
sources.citation: Star Trek Convention (Wikipedia).

entries.title: Elvis, in a hologram, from Hawaii
entries.summary: Elvis Presley was filmed in a two-dimensional process that placed an apparently three-dimensional Elvis on stage, in a scene where real people were supposed to react to him. Aloha from Hawaii via Satellite reached an estimated half the planet.
entries.significance: The first parasocial technology, and it makes the argument nobody wanted to make. It was simultaneously beloved, a triumph, and a demonstration that you can attach to a projection on purpose. Everything since - deepfakes, holograms, an AI voice reading a dead actor's lines - is a lateral move from here.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Aloha from Hawaii via Satellite, 1973

entries.title: Convention culture
entries.summary: Fan conventions as a permanent global circuit, with panels, dealers rooms, cosplay and a trade layer.
entries.significance: The first parasocial economy. Panels are a person answering questions from an audience that has paid to be in the room, and the dealers room is the first marketplace that exists because of the bond rather than beside it.

sources.claim: Comic fandom built its own institution: the Golden State Comic-Con held its first convention in 1970 in a hotel ballroom in San Diego, organised by a group of fans, with Ray Bradbury as the first programme guest. The convention is the fandom's own building
sources.citation: San Diego Comic-Con (Wikipedia).

entries.title: The finding that the satisfaction is not in the show
entries.summary: Across several decades of television studies the same pair of results kept surfacing: these bonds are extremely common among regular viewers, and the strength of the bond predicts enjoyment better than the quality of the programme does.
entries.significance: It says the satisfaction is not in the writing, it is in the accumulation. A show that is not very good, watched consistently, produces a stronger feeling than a good show watched occasionally. This is why commitment to a mediocre series is not a failure of taste, and it is the most consistently replicated and least widely known finding in the entire field.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its individual studies added.

entries.title: The holiday special
entries.summary: A television film made for a fictional holiday, aired once, about characters the audience believed they owned.
entries.significance: The strangest parasocial document in the file. An entire fictional religion, complete with costume, was made for an audience that had formed a genuine attachment, and that audience watched it and understood it as a gift.

sources.claim: Life Day, the Star Wars holiday special, was broadcast on CBS on 17 November 1978 - a holiday invented for a film series, given a network slot, and later quietly dropped. The franchise built a calendar
sources.citation: Life Day (Wikipedia).

entries.title: The uncanny corridor of companionship
entries.summary: The unsettling quality of a humanlike thing that is not human, and the narrow band where it is most compelling.
entries.significance: Predicts the companion era accurately. Too obviously a machine and it is a tool; too obviously a person and it is a person. The uncanny valley is also the commercial sweet spot, which is a genuinely uncomfortable sentence to write.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Mori, 1979

entries.title: The finale study
entries.summary: Academic work measuring grief responses to soap opera finales and finding the same markers as bereavement.
entries.significance: The first hard evidence that a fictional ending produces a real grief response, and the research that was ignored for forty years by a field that had assumed otherwise.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: ABC News, 2023

entries.title: The season finale
entries.summary: Stories resolve on a fixed date, the wait is publicised in advance, and the audience is given a date to be in the same place at the same time.
entries.significance: The modern ritual version of the serial. A year-long shared countdown, with the entire audience aimed at one moment, is the parasocial equivalent of a religious festival and functions identically.

sources.claim: A randomized trial: 44 children assigned to serial (cliffhanger) or episodic delivery of the same story. Serial held engagement across visits; episodic's 'temporary relief' REDUCED long-term play. Unresolved tension beat temporary resolution
sources.citation: To Pause With a Cliffhanger or a Temporary Closure: Serial vs. episodic narratives and sustained engagement.

sources.claim: A cliffhanger is defined in the literature as unresolved tension created specifically to motivate audiences to return to the next episode - the seasonal form of the conduit's promise
sources.citation: To Pause With a Cliffhanger or a Temporary Closure (citing Baranowski et al. 2008; Wirz et al. 2022).

sources.claim: Even failing shows gain viewers for the finale; people who had already stopped watching tune in to find out how it ends. Series finales and Super Bowls are the most-watched broadcasts in US TV history
sources.citation: McCormick, C. TV finales and the meaning of endings (doctoral dissertation).

entries.title: The distance programme
entries.summary: Reward miles accrue against travel, status is conferred by volume, and the first programmes identified their members by searching a booking system for people whose telephone numbers kept recurring.
entries.significance: The least romantic structure on this site and the most revealing, because the first one did the thing this whole file is about and did it in 1981. Texas International is credited with the first frequent flyer programme in 1979; American's AAdvantage followed on 1 May 1981, and American's own newsroom still calls it the first in the world, which is a corporate version of the claim the rest of this site keeps correcting. What matters is how AAdvantage recruited: membership was by invitation only, seeded by searching the SABRE reservations system for recurring telephone numbers, with the 130,000 most frequent flyers pre-enrolled and sent letters carrying their new account numbers. An airline found its regulars inside a computer and wrote to them one at a time. The reward was a first-class ticket to anywhere it flew. United's Mileage Plus arrived within weeks, and the competition that followed is where the language of rank and tier came from - not from aviation but from the arms race between two marketing departments. Every 'personalised' system since is a smaller version of a 1981 letter.

sources.citation: AAdvantage. Wikipedia, citing 'A History of US Airline Deregulation Part 4: 1979-2010: The Effects of Deregulation - Lower Fares, More Travel, Frequent Flier Programs'.
sources.claim: Corrects the entry's date. American launched AAdvantage on 1 May 1981, and it was the *second* such programme in the world, the first being at Texas International Airlines in 1979 - so the entry was two years late. Also the founding detail the entry was standing on top of without describing: membership began by invitation only, and 'membership was seeded by searching American's SABRE computer reservations system for recurring phone numbers', with the 130,000 most frequent flyers plus 60,000 Admirals Club members pre-enrolled and sent letters with their new account numbers, the reward being a first-class ticket to any destination American flew. United launched Mileage Plus within weeks, described as the first *modern* frequent flyer programme; AAdvantage was the first to partner with an international carrier, in 1982.

sources.citation: History of United Airlines. Wikipedia (Mileage Plus, May 1981).
sources.claim: The competitive clock that made the tier system urgent: in May 1981, 'a week after rival American Airlines launched AAdvantage, the first modern frequent flyer program, United launched its Mileage Plus'. Two programmes within days of each other, after which the Wikipedia AAdvantage history notes competition on features began - rules liberalised, hotel and rental partnerships, triple miles from 1988 - which is how a loyalty scheme acquires the language of rank.

entries.title: The supermarket club
entries.summary: A discount card that identifies the household, tracks what it buys, and targets offers at what it has already bought.
entries.significance: The loyalty card joins the account to the person. Everything the field calls the attention economy was operational and profitable in supermarkets a decade before anybody named it.

entries.title: M*A*S*H
entries.summary: Twenty-eight million people watched a television finale and the largest audience for a broadcast in history.
entries.significance: The high-water mark of collective parasocial grief in broadcast television, watched by people who had never met a single person in it. Everything since has been smaller and more numerous.

sources.claim: 'Goodbye, Farewell and Amen' aired 28 February 1983 and drew roughly 105.9 million viewers, about 38 per cent of American households - the most-watched finale in television history at the time. Directed by Alan Alda
