sources.citation: Goodbye, Farewell and Amen (Wikipedia); Nielsen ratings as reported contemporaneously.

sources.claim: A comedy about war that closed by resolving its central question - Korea, the protagonist, the goodbye - and was watched by a third of the country
sources.citation: M*A*S*H (TV series) (Wikipedia).

entries.title: The counter sits between
entries.summary: The person who knows you is also the person who profits from you, and is paid to be there, and goes home at six. The relationship has an employer.
entries.significance: The distinction nobody makes: a parasocial bond feels the same whether the other end is a person, a corporation, a platform or a state. The counter sits between the two, and that middle is where the ethics live. It is also why the video store clerk is the right mascot for a site about this.

entries.title: Parasocial interaction disorder
entries.summary: A clinical name for a case where a one-sided bond is causing significant distress or impairment. Named in the eighties, and it is a real diagnosis for a small number of people.
entries.significance: The trouble is that the disorder and the ordinary bond are the same shape. The disorder requires distress - which means you cannot identify it from the strength of the feeling alone, only by asking what it is costing. That distinction is the whole point, and it is the one most coverage of the subject skips.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Rubin, A. M., McVoy, S. M., & Brannan, D. (1985).

entries.title: Loneliness and local television news
entries.summary: A long-running body of work from Rubin and colleagues, repeatedly finding that people form parasocial bonds with news anchors, and that the strongest predictor of which anchor they bond with is not the anchor's performance.
entries.significance: The finding that broke the standard worry. The parasocial relationship is a substitute for interpersonal contact, not a symptom of pathology, and it does not correlate with poor mental health in the way the disorder framing implies. It is closer to a coping strategy that mostly works.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Rubin, A. M., McVoy, S. M., & Brannan, D. (1985). Human Communication Research, 12(2).

entries.title: The stamp card
entries.summary: Buy nine, get the tenth. A card, a punch, a visible record of loyalty, in the customer's hand.
entries.significance: The most parasocial object in the world and nobody has ever said so. It is a small, portable, accumulating record that a person chooses to carry around, which is functionally an anniversary counter for a café.

sources.claim: The stamp card is a measurable instrument, not a novelty: supermarket loyalty card data has been used to quantify the operational effect of promotions on households rather than on aggregate sales, which is the point at which a discount becomes a profile
sources.citation: Higgs, R., & McInstash, S. (2008). Measuring the operational efficiency of retail promotions which have a loyalty card scheme.

entries.title: The comfort rewatch
entries.summary: The show you have already seen, watched again, not for the plot. Familiarity as a nervous system intervention.
entries.significance: The most functional parasocial behaviour in ordinary life and the one nobody pathologises, because it demonstrably works. Nothing else in a person's week guarantees the outcome. It is also the cleanest evidence that people attach to the accumulation rather than the content.

sources.citation: Grady, S. M., Eden, A., & Wolfers, L. N. (2025). Examining Comfort Media: A Tool for Self-Regulation and Refuge? Mass Communication and Society, 29(2), 245-268.
sources.claim: Comfort media treated as a regulatory instrument rather than a guilty pleasure: the paper builds from media-based coping and recovery research, on the argument that comforting experiences reduce distress the way comfort food does. Supports the summary's 'familiarity as a nervous system intervention', and supports it as a studied effect rather than a received opinion. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request, so marked unverified; volume, issue, pages and authors confirmed against Crossref.

sources.citation: Castle, K. (2019). Comfort TV: Considering Everyday Television Use as a Mode of Self-Care [Data Collection]. University of Glasgow. Datacite DOI: 10.5525/gla.researchdata.798
sources.claim: An audience study of comfort viewing as a mode of self-care, with hospital patients, family units and first-year undergraduates, collecting surveys, two rounds of qualitative interviews and viewing journals (minimum seven entries), collected Oct 2016 - Mar 2017 and released under CC BY 4.0. Establishes that rewatching for comfort has been treated as a coping practice worth a dedicated study including hospital patients - i.e. not pathologised, and taken seriously enough to build a dataset about. Note this record is the data, not the write-up: the findings belong to the thesis and are not claimed here.

entries.title: Is it good for you?
entries.summary: The question underneath all of it, and the reason the clinical literature went in circles for forty years: is a parasocial bond a form of wellbeing, a substitute for it, or neither?
entries.significance: Still unresolved and the most honest place to be. The honest answer is that it depends on cost - money, sleep, peace - rather than on the strength of the feeling, which is why the disorder cannot be identified from the feeling alone and why the audit scores both axes instead of one.

sources.claim: The test this site keeps applying, from the source: whether an arrangement flatters a life is not the question. Aristotle's eudaimonia is activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a whole life - a standard applied to the completed life, not the enjoyable moment
sources.citation: Aristotle. Nicomachean Ethics, Books I and X; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Ethics'.

sources.claim: And the reason the question recurs: the standard is deliberately not reducible to pleasure, which is why an analysis of what makes people feel better about their attachments keeps needing this older vocabulary
sources.citation: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Ethics'.

entries.title: Mourning a person you met
entries.summary: A working vocabulary for grief over a public figure, drawn from bereavement practice, used without qualification.
entries.significance: Adopted slowly and grudgingly. The vocabulary now exists and is mostly used to dismiss people, which is an unfortunate fate for a body of practical advice about a real grief response to a real loss.

sources.claim: The scale of the first known mass grief for a stranger: an estimated 750,000 people at Rudolph Valentino's funeral in 1926 caused destruction at the funeral home
sources.citation: Fan Culture. EBSCO Research Starters, Social Sciences and Humanities.

sources.claim: 'Cofactuality': viewers manage narrative loss by working through and sharing multiple versions of the ending they would have preferred. Grief gets socialised through arguing about what should have happened
sources.citation: McCormick, C. TV finales and the meaning of endings (doctoral dissertation).

sources.claim: The scale of the loss, from the same study: so many viewers equated a presidential farewell address to saying goodbye to a television show that the comparison was drawn in the scholarship
sources.citation: McCormick, C. TV finales and the meaning of endings, citing Peter Brooks.

entries.title: Shipping
entries.summary: Fans insisting two characters should be together, and treating the show as withholding rather than as finished.
entries.significance: The clearest example of a parasocial bond that runs in the opposite direction to the intended one. The audience is not consuming the story, it is running a parallel production about two people who do not exist and are not allowed to.

sources.claim: The practice has its own scholarship and its own naming: pairing characters in the fandom rather than with a real performer is treated as a distinct analytic object, not as fan 'confusion' about which is real
sources.citation: Hills, A. (2014). There's no place for a loli like me in the PLURD community: The liminality of fictional characters and fan identity.

sources.claim: The mechanism is that characters are licensed: a fictional figure can be assigned traits the performer never had, so the attachment does not require the object to behave well
sources.citation: Hills (2014).

entries.title: The stalker statute
entries.summary: Anti-stalking legislation passed in several jurisdictions, defining unwanted repeated contact as a criminal offence.
entries.significance: The first point at which the law acknowledged a parasocial bond can be dangerous to the person at the other end. The offence is about contact, not feeling, which is the correct boundary and the one most online argument resists.

sources.claim: 'Stalking' became a criminal category rather late and for a specific reason: the 1989 murder of actress Rebecca Schaeffer, and the term entered US statutes in the early 1990s, with the UK following in the Protection from Harassment Act 1997. The law arrived after the homicide
sources.citation: Stalking (Wikipedia).

entries.title: The NEST letter
entries.summary: A child writes to a magazine telling them a fictional brand of baby food is real. The NEST never appears. The letter is never answered. The episode ends.
entries.significance: The single most parasocial thing ever put on television, and it is a joke about wanting the writers to confirm that a fictional place is real. An eight-year-old asking to be told the world is real, dressed as a gag about a cereal. Everything on this site happens because a child did not accept the terms.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Rugrats

entries.title: The Power Rangers handover
entries.summary: A costume is put on by a new actor and the audience transfers its entire attachment to whoever is now inside it. Running five days a week, in front of millions of children, with nobody pretending otherwise.
entries.significance: The most complete parasocial handover ever broadcast, and the closest thing television has to a controlled experiment. The audience knew the person had changed. They transferred the feeling anyway, instantly, and enjoyed knowing they were doing it.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Mighty Morphin Power Rangers, 1993-

entries.title: Saturday morning cartoons
entries.summary: A scheduled block, a fixed slot, a face, a voice, a house, a family, and a writer who knows your name. Aimed deliberately at a person old enough to believe all of it, and running on a rhythm.
entries.significance: The clearest parasocial laboratory ever built, and nobody had to design a mechanism because the format is one. A generation went fluent in the vocabulary of attachment here and then explained the internet's emotional economics to people confused by it, and the usual claim - that the internet is making people parasocial - has the timeline exactly backwards.

sources.claim: A whole genre organised around a weekly slot and a captive child audience, and then dismantled by a regulatory decision: children's programming was treated differently from adult broadcasting, so when networks moved their cartoons to weekday mornings the entire appointment-viewing culture went with them
sources.citation: Saturday morning cartoon (Wikipedia).

entries.title: Kurt Cobain
entries.summary: A death broadcast in real time to a generation that had grown up with a songwriter's complaints as a soundtrack.
entries.significance: Parasocial grief with a specific edge: the person had spent years being public about being miserable, and the audience had been treating it as content. Afterwards, every public complaint became a private grief waiting to happen.

sources.claim: THE PARASOCIAL CHANNEL DELIVERED THE DEATH BEFORE THE FAMILY DID. 8 April 1994, around 8:40am, an electrician recognised the body through a window, and called a ROCK RADIO STATION before calling police - because he was a fan. The on-air personality said broadcasting it was 'kind of an eerie decision to make. We're not a news station'
sources.citation: Seattle Times, 8 April 1994; and Rolling Stone (Neil Strauss), Flashback: Kurt Cobain's Last Days.

sources.claim: Cobain's mother and his sister both learned of his death from radio reports. She said: 'Now he's gone and joined that stupid club'
sources.citation: Seattle Times, 8 April 1994.

sources.claim: AND THE EXTRACTION, MEASURED IN HOURS. Two hours after the county medical examiner positively identified the body by fingerprints, most local record stores were completely wiped out of all Nirvana product. One store reported selling a few hundred CDs, singles and vinyl by the next morning, including the $100 interview CD
sources.citation: Carrie Borzillo, When Kurt Cobain Died, Billboard (2019), reporting her 23 April 1994 article 'Cobain Mourned by Fans, Industryites in Memorials, Music Stores'.

sources.claim: Which one record store executive said out loud at the time: 'a pathetic scene. Everything is going out the door. If people were really fans, they'd have had this stuff already.' The industry diagnosing the fans while taking their money
sources.citation: Tower Records' Chris Simmons, quoted in Billboard (2019), April 1994.

sources.claim: The scale of the assembly: roughly 5,000 people at the public memorial at the Flag Pavilion near the Space Needle on 10 April 1994, at which Courtney Love - by tape - asked the crowd to shout 'asshole' at the man they had just grieved
sources.citation: Borzillo, Billboard (2019); Rolling Stone (1994).

sources.claim: And a fan's own account of the mechanism, on the street outside his house: 'Nirvana touched something deep inside me'
sources.citation: Seattle Times, 8 April 1994, reporting Laura Mitchell.

sources.claim: The counter-claim, and it is the strongest version of the other side: 'He was his audience' - the songs were written from experience the listeners recognised as their own
sources.citation: MTV News Special Report, The Life & Death of Kurt Cobain (1994), reporting Michael Azerrad.

entries.title: The character death
entries.summary: Killing a popular character for narrative effect, and the organised reaction that follows.
entries.significance: The most reliable audience manipulation in fiction, because it is the only one the audience cannot avoid. Grief engineered as a plot device is the writer's oldest trick and the fandom's most reliable grievance.

sources.claim: n=840: both the positivity of a main character's outcome and perceived narrative closure were associated with reduced emotional distress - depression, anger, anxiety. Ending well measurably lowers the damage
sources.citation: Krakowiak, K. M. (2024). How It Ends.

sources.claim: Produced for finale-hype: producers craft a deliberate path to closure, and the anticipation of the end then shapes the entire final season retroactively
sources.citation: McCormick, C. TV finales and the meaning of endings (doctoral dissertation).

entries.title: The companion bot boom
entries.summary: Dozens of scripted personalities, rememberers, and subscription companions sold to a mass market in the mid-nineties.
entries.significance: The commercial attempt that came twenty-five years before it worked. The category has the same name, the same promise, and a very different population, and comparing the two eras is instructive about what the internet added.

sources.claim: ELIZA, 1966, and its programmer's founding complaint: that people insisted on believing the machine understood them when it did not - 'the user is the interpreter'. Every attachment since is a variation on the error ELISA's author found unbearably moving
sources.citation: ELIZA (Wikipedia); Weizenbaum, J. (1966). ELIZA - A computer program for the study of natural language communication between man and machine.

entries.title: Clerks beat algorithms
entries.summary: The difference between being known by somebody who was paying attention on purpose and being modelled by a system that has your history. Same information, different relationship.
entries.significance: The distinction the whole site turns on. A clerk who notices what you rented has one motive - you coming back. An algorithm optimising for watch time has yours, but it does not know what you rented. The second is not better at caring. It is better at correlating, and the human experience of the difference is the entire subject.

entries.title: The loyalty counter
entries.summary: Points, tiers, an anniversary date, a number that has been going up for years, and the quiet threat of what happens to it if you leave. The most ordinary parasocial object ever invented.
entries.significance: It converts a relationship into an account, and an account is something with a balance. Nobody feels moved by a balance. The remarkable thing is how much feeling the machinery of a balance can carry once you have also attached to a person - the anniversary counter is not a relationship, it is a receipt for one.

sources.claim: What the card buys the retailer: a per-household purchase history, which is what makes a 'personalised recommendation' possible and what turns a discount into surveillance with a discount attached
sources.citation: Higgs, R., & McInstash, S. (2008). Measuring the operational efficiency of retail promotions which have a loyalty card scheme.

sources.claim: And the retention design, which is the reason leaving is hard: the same paper measures effects at household level, so the relationship being managed is the household's basket, not the shopper's satisfaction
sources.citation: Higgs & McInstash (2008).

entries.title: The brand that has a personality
entries.summary: Corporations given a voice, a face, a founder narrative, and a tone, so that a customer relationship has a subject.
entries.significance: The final move of the parasocial relationship into commerce: the thing you have feelings about is a legal person. Brands now do this deliberately and in the open, and it is the completion of a process that started with a singer.

sources.claim: THE CITATION THIS ENTRY WAS WAITING FOR. A peer-reviewed study of what happens when a narrative brand ends: narrative closure and 'consumption sociality' on loss accommodation. A character that is also a brand does not get to die quietly
sources.citation: Russell, C. A., & Schau, H. J. (2013). When Narrative Brands End: The Impact of Narrative Closure and Consumption Sociality on Loss Accommodation. Journal of Consumer Research, 40(6), 1039-1062.

entries.title: The boy band
entries.summary: Bands assembled for a market, with fan clubs, fan voting, fan merchandise and fan-financed releases.
entries.significance: Fandom reorganised as an economic instrument. The fan stopped being an audience and became a funding mechanism, which is the single most consequential change in the whole file.

sources.claim: A manufactured category with a manufacturing process: Popstars: The Rivals (2000) let a panel choose rather than audition, and the resulting groups were assembled rather than found. The boy band is the star system with the mystique removed and the volume raised
sources.citation: Boy band (Wikipedia); Popstars: The Rivals (2000).

entries.title: Webcasting
entries.summary: Streaming video over a network, at first unbroadcast and unproduced, from a bedroom or a desk.
entries.significance: The medium that removed the gatekeeper before it removed the schedule. Everything a creator economy is today existed in this form first, badly, and was not interesting to anybody.

sources.claim: Webcasting - streaming live audio and video over the internet - went mainstream in the mid-1990s, with RealAudio in 1995 and the 1995 relaunch of Justin and Eric's site as the first widely recognised example. Before it, a performance was a place you had to be
sources.citation: Webcasting (Wikipedia).

entries.title: The anime import boom
entries.summary: Japanese animation and comics reach a large Western audience through dedicated channels, and a transnational fandom forms around them.
entries.significance: Fandom stops being national and starts being organised around translation, release schedules and convention circuits. The parasocial bond acquires logistics, which is how you can tell it is real.

sources.claim: Anime as imported mass attachment: American television carried Japanese animation from the 1960s, and a later wave - Voltron, the Ninja Turtles, Dragon Ball - made the form available to people who never read the original in translation. The conduit crossed languages without asking permission
sources.citation: Anime in the United States (Wikipedia).

entries.title: Forum culture
entries.summary: Persistent text spaces with per-topic cultures, norms enforced by social pressure and volume.
entries.significance: Where the pile-on was invented. Fandom moved from letters to threads, and a thread has thousands of people in it at once with no moderator and no cost to replying.

sources.claim: Stan Twitter works as a functioning Community of Practice: members form interpersonal bonds, communicate regularly, and contribute. A fan forum is a real community, not a comment box
sources.citation: Malik, Z., & Haidar, S. (2020). Online community development through social interaction - K-Pop stan twitter as a community of practice. Interactive Learning Environments, 31(2).

entries.title: The sasaeng
entries.summary: A fan whose attachment has become fixed, repeated and physical: tracking whereabouts, intercepting flights, surveilling buildings. The word is Korean and the practice is not new, but the scale and the criminality are.
entries.significance: The point at which the fiction ends being a fiction. It is also the lane's honest boundary: the same feeling, the same industry, the same platforms, and a line that once gets crossed cannot be uncrossed by anyone in the room. Convictions for stalking a member of a group have followed this pattern in several jurisdictions.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its sources added.

entries.title: Sasaeng culture
entries.summary: Organised, commercialised intrusion: tracking schedules, buying flight details, intercepting travel, surveilling buildings.
entries.significance: Attachment scaled past the point where it is a private feeling and became an industry with staff and infrastructure. The escalation is not emotional, it is logistical - which is why it emerged as fandom became globally coordinated.

sources.claim: THE MECHANISM: fans know far more about the celebrity than the reverse, which lets them disrupt the relationship and gain a temporary sense of power and self-efficacy. Ethnogographic study with interviews
sources.citation: Nanyang Business School, NTU Singapore (2017). The Darker Side of K-pop?

sources.claim: The term: sa (private) + saeng (life), intrusion into celebrities' private lives. Behaviour emerges with 1990s K-pop idol groups, not with the digital era
sources.citation: Sasaeng fan. Wikipedia.

sources.claim: The law followed the behaviour: the Kim Changwan case, stalked over ten years, produced a 'persistent harassment' offence added to the Minor Offences Act in 2011, revised 2013, and a 2016 bill raising the maximum penalty
sources.citation: Sasaeng fan. Wikipedia, citing the statute history.

sources.claim: A peer-reviewed typology of True Fan / Ani-Fan / Sasaeng, which states that parasocial relationship is central to the Korean pop culture industry and examines its top-down structuring of the fan-object bond
sources.citation: The Spectrum of Fan Attitudes in Korean Culture Industry (2022).

sources.claim: The global parallel: sasaeng behaviour exported, and doxxing as the anglophone equivalent - plus the gendered stigma attached to female fandom
sources.citation: Khedun-Burgoine, B. 'How do I Make Oppa Sarang Me?': Resemiotisation and Reconstruction of Meaning in the Global K-pop Fandom. University of Oxford ORA.

entries.title: Transparasocial interaction
entries.summary: The 1990s extension to live people who respond in real time - streamers, hosts, people who read your comment. The bond is still fundamentally one-sided, but the other side can now hear you.
entries.significance: The term that made the field relevant to the internet, and the reason the word changed: the phenomenon did not, only the possibility of contact. It is the same bond with the floor removed, which is why it feels better and goes wrong faster.

sources.claim: The entry as a whole: transparasocial interaction as it is actually used in the literature - a one-sided bond with a live performer whose audience can be heard in real time, studied on Twitch. The DOI is confirmed against Crossref metadata, but the publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request, so this is recorded as unverified rather than pretending the text was read.
sources.citation: Carter, A. E., & Hoy, M. G. (2024). We're All Friends Here: Examining Transparasocial Interaction on Twitch and Its Effects on Strategic Communications. Journal of Interactive Advertising, 24(2), 127-142.

entries.title: Transnational fandom
entries.summary: Fans organising across national borders around media, with a shared calendar of releases and a shared language.
entries.significance: Fandom became infrastructure. When a release date is a global event and the discourse is synchronised across time zones, the parasocial bond stops being a private thing and becomes a public holiday.

sources.claim: The canonical account of fandom as crossing borders and refusing to stay in its box: Jenkins, *Convergence Culture* (2006), and the scholarship that followed on K-pop, anime and football travelling further than the industry intended
sources.citation: Jenkins, H. (2006). Convergence Culture: Where Old and New Media Collide.

entries.title: The reality celebrity
entries.summary: A person famous for being filmed, with no skill, no work and no release schedule - and an audience that formed anyway.
entries.significance: The purest parasocial figure ever mainstreamed: fame with no product, only proximity. It also removed the last barrier - you no longer need to be good at anything, you only need to be watched.

sources.claim: The format originated as an unembodied surveillance experiment and produced celebrity from it: the Dutch precursor De Teleboom began in 1997, watched by a studio audience who dialled in votes, and the format was exported worldwide from 2000
sources.citation: Big Brother (franchise) (Wikipedia).

entries.title: Second Life
entries.summary: A persistent virtual world with avatars, economies, and relationships between people who never met.
entries.significance: Parasocial attachment with a body and a social graph, and the first virtual environment where the loneliness was addressed directly rather than incidentally. It also produced the first convention-attendance problem in a space with no physical convention.

sources.claim: Measured on a validated attachment scale with 125 Second Life residents: attachments formed in the virtual world are EQUALLY STRONG as those in real life. The virtual bond is not a diluted version of the real one
sources.citation: Quackenbush, D. M., Allen, J. G., & Fowler, J. C. Comparison of Attachments in Real-World and Virtual-World Relationships.

sources.claim: AND THE PART THAT IS NOT A DILUTION: attachment anxiety is LOWER in virtual-world relationships than real ones. Emotional wellbeing tracks strength of attachment in the real world and low anxiety in the virtual one
sources.citation: Quackenbush, Allen & Fowler, Comparison of Attachments in Real-World and Virtual-World Relationships.

sources.claim: A regulator's finding on what an avatar is: the avatar is 'a symbol of the self, representing the user's deepest wishes, aspirations, virtues and vices', and for some players becomes a purposeful projection or idealisation of identity, for others an experiment in being someone new
sources.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008). Second Life: Privacy in Virtual Worlds.

sources.claim: N=236, recruited inside Second Life, every participant in a committed real-world relationship: 81.7% also had a committed virtual relationship with a DIFFERENT partner, and no real-life relationship was significantly more satisfying than any Second Life relationship in any statistical analysis
sources.citation: Kolotkin, R. A., Williams, M. M., Lloyd, C., & Hallford, E. W. Does Loving an Avatar Threaten Real Life Marriage?

sources.claim: And the asymmetry in how it lands: women tended to define their Second Life relationships as significantly MORE satisfying than their real ones; men as equally satisfying
sources.citation: Kolotkin, Williams, Lloyd & Hallford, Does Loving an Avatar Threaten Real Life Marriage?

sources.claim: The capability this entry describes, treated as an experimental asset by researchers: face-to-face communication with full non-verbal cues while never compromising real-world anonymity
sources.citation: The lab versus the virtual lab and virtual field - an experimental investigation of trust games with communication (Second Life).

entries.title: Michael Jackson
entries.summary: Died 25 June 2009, and within hours the crowd at his house was described by a firefighter as a circus, with tour buses at the gate. By August the coroner had called it a homicide and the autopsy was sealed.
entries.significance: The moment grief for a parasocial figure became a media product, and the date is the argument. Reported first as a rumour, confirmed through the coroner two hours later, with a publicist on record the same night and a prime-time documentary already in the same news cycle. Speculation about the cause was running before the autopsy had begun, and the autopsy and toxicology reports were then held under seal - which is the mechanism: an audience cannot be given the fact, so the coverage sells the waiting. The line between honouring the dead and selling the death was drawn that week and it was not respected. It has since become routine: this is the template that every later death of a public figure followed.

sources.citation: Grigsby Bates, K. (2009, June 25). Michael Jackson Dead At 50: The Two-Way. NPR.
sources.claim: Fixes the date: Jackson died on Thursday 25 June 2009 at UCLA Medical Center, pronounced dead at 2:26pm, aged 50. Also documents the entry's actual subject from inside the first hours: TMZ reported the death first and CNN confirmed it more than two hours later via the Los Angeles coroner, and the publicist who had served Jackson during the 1991 molestation trial issued a statement to assembled reporters within the first night, describing him as 'impossibly difficult and often self-destructive'. Grief and access arriving as a media product, hours after the news, with no cooling-off period.

sources.citation: Duke, A. (2009, August 28). Michael Jackson's death was a homicide, coroner rules. CNN.
sources.claim: The investigation that followed, which is what turned the mourning into sustained coverage: the Los Angeles County coroner ruled the death a homicide, finding propofol and lorazepam the primary drugs responsible, with midazolam, diazepam, lidocaine and ephedrine also detected, and cited 'acute propofol intoxication' with 'benzodiazepine effect' as a contributing condition. The full autopsy and toxicology reports were placed on security hold at the request of police and the district attorney, and federal and state agencies opened parallel investigations.

sources.citation: ABC News (2019, June 13). 'My God, Michael Jackson is dead': The final hours leading up to the pop star's death.
sources.claim: The scene at the house, from a firefighter-paramedic who was there: the ambulance leaving the Holmby Hills home was met, in his words, by 'a circus' - 'Paparazzi... people, tourists. There was even a double-decker tour bus' - and a celebrity bus tour was stopped by emergency personnel on the way out. This is the entry's 'line between honouring the dead and selling the death', witnessed by someone who was working.

sources.citation: Nasaw, D., & Wood, B. (2009, June 26). Michael Jackson dies: worldwide reaction (live). The Guardian.
sources.claim: Live reporting from the first morning, showing the mechanics the entry describes: speculation about the cause circulating within hours (including a report that he was addicted to Demerol), the coroner saying at 3:51pm that the autopsy would begin 'in minutes' with no definitive results expected for six to eight weeks, and the 1970s-edition of a prime-time documentary being discussed in the same news cycle.

entries.title: Fighting about a stranger in a reply section
entries.summary: A disagreement conducted entirely in good faith about a person none of the participants have met, using the vocabulary of a personal grievance.
entries.significance: A parasocial relationship conducted in public with a complete stranger, and the argument is never about the stranger. The people with the strongest feelings are the most likely to be drawn in, which is the same property that makes fandoms work.

sources.claim: Fighting about a stranger is norm enforcement, not expression: accusation triggers moral outrage, the network piles on, and the target self-censors. Interviews n=28 plus n=9 Trust and Safety workers
sources.citation: Marwick, A. E. Morally Motivated Networked Harassment as Normative Reinforcement.

sources.claim: Sanctioning a stranger is an identity signal, and is read as one by everyone watching
sources.citation: Ahn, C., Lelkes, Y., & Levendusky, M. S. (2024). Sanctioning political speech on social media is driven by partisan norms and identity signaling.

entries.title: Doxxing the person, not the character
entries.summary: The jump from disliking a fictional portrayal to locating and publishing a real person's address. The word had to be invented for a grievance that used to be settled by writing a letter.
entries.significance: The escalation everyone predicted and nobody predicted the timing of. Note what the parasocial frame does here: the audience is not attached to the person being targeted, they are attached to somebody playing them. The harm lands on a human who did not choose to be a character.

sources.claim: Organised exposure of personal information used as a campaign tactic rather than incidental doxxing, documented as a distinct practice and separately criminalised in a number of jurisdictions
sources.citation: Doxxing (Wikipedia).

entries.title: The crowd injury
entries.summary: Fans are injured or killed attempting to get closer to a performer, in volume, repeatedly, for years.
entries.significance: Direct physical risk from proximity-seeking, and the clearest line where attachment stops being a private matter and becomes somebody else's liability.

sources.claim: 5 November 2021, Astroworld, Houston: ten deaths in a crowd crush, with the fatal bottleneck forming while attendees were still recording and posting to social media from inside it. The audience was filming the audience being injured
sources.citation: Astroworld Festival (Wikipedia).

entries.title: The character is not the person
entries.summary: The pattern of locating and publishing a private address over a disliked fictional portrayal.
entries.significance: Escalation past the point of no return, and the reason the whole lane needs to exist rather than being left off the site as uncomfortable. The public is not attached to the person being targeted, which is the detail that makes it indefensible.

sources.claim: Doxxing and public shaming are the standard repertoire of morally motivated networked harassment (n=28 targets, n=9 platform Trust and Safety staff)
sources.citation: Marwick, A. E. Morally Motivated Networked Harassment as Normative Reinforcement.

sources.claim: People judge harassment MORE justified and more deserved - though not more appropriate - when the target has done something. Retribution drives it (n=160, n=432)
sources.citation: Blackwell, L., Chen, T., Schoenebeck, S., & Lampe, C. When Online Harassment Is Perceived as Justified. ICWSM.

entries.title: The goodwill gesture
entries.summary: When a service ends or changes, the company sends an apology, sometimes with credit, addressed personally.
entries.significance: A corporation performing grief at its own users, correctly, because the users are grieving - and the best-documented case says so back. Google Reader launched in 2005, which is where this entry's date comes from; Google retired it on 1 July 2013 with 'Thanks for 8 great years', and an engineer added that Reader had a devoted following who would be very sad to see it go and that Google was sad too. Forty-six thousand people signed a petition within hours, and its author had already found the grammar: 'This isn't just about our data in Reader. This is about us using your product because we love it, because it makes our lives better, and because we trust you not to nuke it.' One user grieved not the product but himself: 'I won't miss Reader when it shuts down. But I will miss the old me - the person I described in Google Reader, without knowing it.' The reason the technique is free, and the reason it works, is the same and it is in the record: Reader was never monetised. No ads, no charge, feeds that were hard to make money from. The apology cost nothing because the relationship it was performed for was one Google had never sold anything to.

sources.citation: Gross, D. (2013, March 14). Google Reader shutting down on July 1. CNN Business.
sources.claim: The mechanism, its vocabulary, and the detail the entry's argument depends on. Google's line: 'We know Reader has a devoted following who will be very sad to see it go. We're sad too.' Within hours more than 46,000 people had signed a Change.org petition, and its author stated the entry's thesis outright: 'This isn't just about our data in Reader. This is about us using your product because we love it, because it makes our lives better, and because we trust you not to nuke it.' And the commercial fact underneath it: 'The feeds are also difficult to make money from, and Google never tried to place ads on Reader or charge for its use.'

sources.citation: Rothman, J. (2013, March 15). Farewell, Dear Reader. The New Yanker's Page-Turner.
sources.claim: The grief, and its object. A user describes Reader as the first site he saw each morning and the last before bed, likens losing it to a favourite old bookshop closing, and then locates the real loss precisely: 'I won't miss Reader when it shuts down. But I will miss the old me - the person I described in Google Reader, without knowing it.' Which is this site's grief entry turned inside out: what was mourned was not the company but a version of the person who had used it.

sources.citation: Sottek, T. (2013, March 13). Google Closes The Book On Google Reader On July 1. TechCrunch.
sources.claim: The service's own send-off and the reason given: Reader launched in 2005, would be retired on 1 July 2013, and Google told users 'Thanks for 8 great years!' - which is where this entry's 2005 date comes from. Usage had declined while other services were cut in the same spring cleaning, and Reader had been left without significant updates.

entries.title: YouTube launches
entries.summary: Uploads become trivially cheap and the audience begins to attach to individuals rather than channels.
entries.significance: Attachment shifts from institutions to people at exactly the point the distribution cost goes to zero. The broadcaster's ten-year relationship with a channel becomes a viewer's ten-year relationship with a face.

sources.claim: Founded 14 February 2005 as a side project by four people, one of whom later described it as a hobby with the feature set of a TV channel. The first upload was 'Me at the zoo'; it passed a million users by the end of 2005
sources.citation: YouTube (Wikipedia).

entries.title: The phone becomes a person
entries.summary: Roughly half a billion phone numbers become dialable, a fan can in principle hear a recorded voice, and the novelty ringtone sells the idea that a performer can be present in a pocket for about four years.
entries.significance: The real discontinuity, and a much narrower one than the standard story. The feeling was not new; the possibility of contact was. The reply is now structurally impossible in a way a letter never was - an email is not paper, it does not have to be opened, and the person reading it has a thousand. The conditions that made a reply work were small enough for one human to hold, and they are gone permanently.

sources.claim: THE PHONE AS A PERSON, MEASURED. Idol messaging apps are described in the literature as simulating parasocial interaction by allowing one-to-one texting with a performer, deepening the 'intensification' stage of attachment. Every user who used one said it increased their sense of connection
sources.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans, citing Aw & Chua (2021), Kim & Song (2016), Bond (2016).

sources.claim: Verbatim, from a 14-18 year old: 'It (Weverse) makes me feel like I'm talking to one of my best friends.' That is the whole entry, said by someone who had no vocabulary for it
sources.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans.

entries.title: The pile-on
entries.summary: Enforcement by volume: a position is declared untenable, a pile of people makes it so, and the outcome is a fact nobody chose.
entries.significance: Governance without authority. There is no court, no evidence standard and no appeal, only a critical mass of people who can agree, and the person on the losing end has the same parasocial attachment as everyone else and is treated as the problem.

sources.claim: The mechanism: people are reluctant to be the FIRST to sanction anyone, but pile on once others have acted. Three experiments.
sources.citation: Ahn, C., Lelkes, Y., & Levendusky, M. S. (2024). Sanctioning political speech on social media is driven by partisan norms and identity signaling.

sources.claim: Pile-ons are learned, not spontaneous: positive social feedback for outrage raises future outrage, and users conform to their network's expressive norm
sources.citation: Brady, N., et al. (2021). How social learning amplifies moral outrage expression in online social networks. Science Advances, 7(28), eabe5641.

sources.claim: The outrage-mob shape, stated plainly: a few condemn, then more pile on with little regard for evidence (n=10,343)
sources.citation: How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking. (2023).

entries.title: The actor and the character
entries.summary: An actor's persona and a character's persona are widely treated as the same thing, and one retires while the other continues.
entries.significance: The cleanest test of whether a parasocial bond attaches to a person or a role, and the answer changes depending on who is asked. The character outlives the actor, which is evidence for the fiction and against the man.

sources.citation: Frye, J. (2013, May 3). Iron Man Unmasked: Robert Downey Jr., Don Cheadle & More Talk Character. The Credits, Motion Picture Association of America. (Courtesy of the Walt Disney Company.)
sources.claim: The entry's question asked directly of the people who made the thing, rather than inferred from fan behaviour. Kevin Feige: 'How do you take a billionaire, industrialist playboy and make him relatable and somebody that you can root for?' and, on the alternative, 'take everything away from the character, which then makes you root for the guy'. Stephen Broussard on the boundary itself: even though the world knows and loves Tony Stark, 'he is still learning and struggling to define where Iron Man ends and his own life begins'. The unresolvable seam between persona and persona is named here by the people controlling it.

entries.title: The Bieber effect
entries.summary: A performer with no media infrastructure becomes a global star through a video-sharing platform alone.
entries.significance: This entry used to call it a parasocial bond formed with no gatekeeper whatsoever, and there were three. Scooter Braun found the videos by accidentally clicking one while looking for another singer; Usher signed him to Island Def Jam after a bidding war; and he was crowned in the same stroke in the venerable line of Tiger Beat's Leifs and Shauns, with his own mother uploading the videos to his channel. What the case actually marks is the discovery layer coming apart - a twelve-year-old's bedroom covers reaching a promoter with no audition, no A&R, and no gate - while the business immediately reassembled around him. The honest version is more interesting than the myth: for one window the middle of the old machine was missing, and the attachments of that window were adopted wholesale. The proof is not a chart position but a cancelled booking - a November 2009 mall appearance called off because of an out-of-control crowd of teenage girls, which is the point at scale. Two numbers in the old version were also wrong: the platform was two to four years old, not fourteen, and the attachment was a year or two, with the record that carried him everywhere arriving in January 2010, just after the entry's date.

sources.citation: Justin Bieber Fast Facts. CNN.
sources.claim: The sequence, which is three gatekeepers rather than none. 2007-2008: 'Bieber's mother begins posting videos of her son performing on YouTube. Record executive Scooter Braun sees the videos and flies Bieber and his mother to Atlanta and signs the teen to a contract.' 2008: auditions for Usher and is signed to Island/Def Jam. May 2009: 'One Time'. November 2009: the My World EP. Also the detail the entry was missing: in November 2009 an appearance at Roosevelt Field Mall in New York 'must be canceled due to an out-of-control crowd of teen girls' - a parasocial mass event inside the entry's own year, rather than a chart position.

sources.citation: Adib, D. (2009, November 14). Pop Star Justin Bieber Is on the Brink of Superstardom. ABC News.
sources.claim: Bieber's own account of the discovery layer, and the part that bypassed it: posting homemade covers from the age of twelve, 'It had a hundred views, then a thousand views, then ten thousand views, so I just kept posting more videos and more videos'. The piece also makes the chain explicit by comparison - 'Usher had "Star Search" to launch him out of obscurity at age 13. His new protege, Justin Bieber, had YouTube' - and records a bidding war, with Timberlake also interested before Usher won him for Island Def Jam.

entries.title: The attention economy
entries.summary: The shift from selling things to selling attention, which means the commodity being bought is a person's feeling - and the seller is whoever is on the other end of it.
entries.significance: It gives the parasocial question its economic form. Once attention is the product, the parasocial bond is not a side effect of the business model, it is the business model. Every mechanism in the manipulation lane is a technique for converting affection into measurable minutes.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Wu, T. (2016). The Attention Merchants.

entries.title: The lobby
entries.summary: A fan harmed in an attempt to breach a celebrity's home, and a petition that followed.
entries.significance: The moment international fandom organised as an advocacy body, and the moment it was clear that a fandom can be a political actor with a legal strategy. The petition was both a moral position and an extremely effective piece of marketing for the industry.

entries.title: The dark pattern in the loyalty card
entries.summary: Exploiting the sunk cost of an earned balance: expiry, devaluation, tier demotion, and the deliberate design of loss.
entries.significance: Everything the field calls manipulation, expressed in the vocabulary of retail. The expiry date on a points balance is a grief event with a date on it, and it is engineered to occur annually.

sources.claim: THE SUNK COST FALLACY, NAMED AS A DESIGN TECHNIQUE. 'Hidden Costs' reveals new charges immediately before purchase; the paper states this exploits the sunk cost fallacy - users feel so invested they justify the extra charge to avoid wasting their effort. The loyalty card is this
sources.citation: Mathur, A., Acar, G., Friedman, M. J., Lucherini, E., Mayer, J., Chetty, M., & Narayanan, A. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 3(CSCW), Article 81.

sources.claim: The asymmetry, stated as a category: it is easy to sign up for recurring subscriptions and memberships, but hard to cancel. 'Hard to Cancel' found on 31 websites
sources.citation: Mathur et al. (2019), citing Gray et al. (2018) taxonomy; pattern originally Brignull's Roach Motel.

sources.claim: Scale, and the part that indicts the industry: 1,818 dark pattern instances across 15 types and 7 categories on 1,254 of ~11,000 shopping websites (11.1%), with 234 instances on 183 websites exhibiting deceptive behaviour. More popular sites were MORE likely to feature them. And 22 third-party entities sell dark patterns as a turnkey solution
sources.citation: Mathur et al. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale.

sources.claim: How hard: unsubscribing from Bloomberg took TEN clicks and required launching and conversing with a closed-domain chatbot first. Cancelling required entering first and last name into the chatbot welcome page, declining discount offers, answering a question to confirm, and completing a mandatory exit survey
sources.citation: Staying at the Roach Motel: Cross-Country Analysis of Manipulative Subscription and Cancellation Flows (2024).

sources.claim: Confirmation as a toll: The Daily Wire required a three-question mandatory survey AND typing the word 'CONFIRM' to cancel. The authors concede some friction prevents accidents, and note that requiring a typed phrase appears unnecessary
sources.citation: Staying at the Roach Motel (2024).

sources.claim: The harm is process harm: study of 53 Indian apps found 52 carried at least one deceptive pattern and e-commerce ran 5.3 per app against 2.7 across sectors, and argues the resulting regret is PROCESS regret from a bad decision procedure, not outcome regret from a bad product - which is why satisfaction metrics miss it
sources.citation: Dark Patterns in Indian E-Commerce Interfaces and Consumer Purchase Regret. Research Review Journal of Social Science.

sources.claim: It is now law, not preference: India's CCPA notified Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns on 30 November 2023, declaring thirteen practices unfair trade practices under the Consumer Protection Act 2019. The EU Digital Services Act uses the term 'dark patterns' officially
sources.citation: Dark Patterns in Indian E-Commerce Interfaces and Consumer Purchase Regret, citing CCPA (2023) and DSA (2022).

entries.title: Paid intimacy
entries.summary: Paid message apps where a window shaped exactly like the one holding your best friend costs about four dollars a month per artist, plus anniversary counters that make the bond feel cumulative and streaks that convert it into a hostage situation.
entries.significance: The lane where the feeling is genuine and the design is not accidental. Every mechanism here was tested, found to work, and shipped. The person is not being scammed, which is exactly what makes it difficult - the affection is real and so is the invoice, and the industry is extremely good at keeping those two facts in separate mental drawers.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its series added.

entries.title: The quarterly audit
entries.summary: The only intervention on this site that you do to yourself, and the only one nobody else can do for you. List your five strongest one-sided ties, score joy and cost, keep three, mute one, trade one hour a week toward a person in the room.
entries.significance: Not a cure and not a diagnostic. A rebalancing, done badly, about four times a year. It exists because the seventh law is the only part of the field that is actually yours, and because the numbers - one to ten, twice - make a feeling arguable.

entries.title: Grief merchandise
entries.summary: Apparel, prints and objects released after a death, quickly, at a profit.
entries.significance: The commercial form of parasocial grief, and nobody involved pretends otherwise any more. It also sustains a cottage industry of people whose entire output is the deaths of people they never met.

sources.claim: The commercial record of the immediate aftermath, in the trade press, in the same week: Billboard ran 'Cobain Mourned by Fans, Industryites in Memorials, Music Stores' on 23 April 1994 - memorials and merchandise as a single subject
sources.citation: Borzen/Borzillo, Billboard (2019), reporting the 23 April 1994 article.

sources.claim: And the deadline in which it must happen: within two hours of positive identification, the retail market for his work was empty. Grief merchandise has a shelf life measured in hours
sources.citation: Borzillo, Billboard (2019).

entries.title: Watching the replies
entries.summary: The public performance of being at war with somebody, in public, for an audience, in a thread that never closes.
entries.significance: A parasocial relationship conducted with a second parasocial relationship attached - you are performing the fight for the room, not having it with the person. The room is the relationship and the person is the prop.

entries.title: The recurring delivery
entries.summary: A monthly box of chosen items, an unboxing ritual, and a personal recommendation from somebody with taste.
entries.significance: The clerk behind a counter, automated and shipped monthly. The whole appeal is that a person chose this for you, and the whole trick is that the choice was made by a recommendation system.

sources.claim: THE ENTRY'S MECHANISM, MEASURED. A controlled experiment (n=144) found unboxing COMPLEXITY has a main effect on positive affect (beta=.53, p=.020), and that positive affect in turn significantly increases willingness to share, online and off. The ritual is the product
sources.citation: Berden, C. Thinking inside the box: the effect of the unboxing experience on positive affect and willingness to share (University of Twente MSc thesis).

sources.claim: The scale of the ritual: an estimated 2.35 MILLION unboxing videos of the iPhone 6 were uploaded to YouTube in 2014, and about a quarter of a million were dedicated to a single subscription box brand. Unboxing became a genre with an audience
sources.citation: Berden, Thinking inside the box, citing Bayston (2016).

sources.claim: And it is treated as engineering, not whimsy: Apple designer Jonathan Ives on the practice - 'You design a ritual of unpacking to make the product feel special. Packaging can be theatre, it can create a story' - and the company tests hundreds of package designs in a dedicated unboxing room
sources.citation: Berden, Thinking inside the box, citing Forbes (2014) and Mashable (2012).

sources.claim: THE PART THAT IS ACTUALLY DISTURBING. An eye-tracking lab experiment found personalization improves the customer experience EVEN WHEN THE CUSTOMER DOES NOT PERCEIVE IT. Actual personalization shifts objective behaviour - attention concentrates on favoured products and they are more likely to be selected - while only perceived personalization moves subjective feelings
sources.citation: Personalization and playful customer experience, with eye-tracking (Universite catholique de Louvain).

sources.claim: The recommendation is the relationship: participants in a 2025 study emphasised the stylist or curator as the thing delivering the value, with algorithms used in the stylist's absence. Stylists keep notes, reference past purchases, and are trusted with items the subscriber says they would never have chosen
sources.citation: Bhatt, D. (2025). Consumers' perceptions towards subscription retail: a focus on online fashion box services.

sources.claim: And what participants named as the risks, unprompted: inability to opt out when not using the service, the time cost of interacting with a stylist, and the environmental cost of packaging and shipping. The convenience and the exit are the same design decision
sources.citation: Bhatt (2025), citing Tao & Xu (2017).

sources.claim: The shape of the relationship, named from 26 in-depth interviews: a subscription box journey has three stages - INITIATION, IMMERSION and EGRESS - each adding to or subtracting from utilitarian and hedonic value. Renewal and cancellation are stages of the same stream, not opposite decisions
sources.citation: Alba, J. W. Navigating consumption streams: Toward a utilitarian-hedonic perspective on subscription box customer journeys. Journal of Consumer Behaviour.

entries.title: Nobody answered
entries.summary: The schedule goes from weekly to continuous and the bond loses its shape. A serial gives you a slot and a cliffhanger; an always-on feed has no slot and no gap to miss anybody in.
entries.significance: The rhythm was doing work nobody had measured. What replaced it is a permanent low-grade availability, which is a different emotional object: not a person who is more present, but one who is never finished, so there is no gap and therefore nothing to miss anybody in. The half of this the evidence supports is the gap - parasocial scales built in this period ask directly whether you miss characters when a show is between seasons, which is the thing an always-on feed removes. The other half it does not: where this entry's argument used to be that the bond loses its shape, the one controlled test of that mechanism found the bond getting *stronger*. Removing the slot does not obviously weaken the tie. It removes the absence, and the site has no evidence about what that costs.

sources.citation: Erickson, S., Dal Cin, S., & Byl, H. (2019). An Experimental Examination of Binge Watching and Narrative Engagement. Social Sciences, 8(1), 19.
sources.claim: Binge watching was experimentally manipulated, not merely correlated, and the reported result runs the OPPOSITE way to this entry's argument: it increased the strength of parasocial relationships and the intensity of narrative transportation. So the claim that the bond 'loses its shape' when the weekly rhythm is removed is this site's position, and the one controlled test of it found the bond getting stronger. Recorded rather than smoothed over. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request; authors, volume, issue and article number confirmed against Crossref.

sources.citation: Anghelcev, G., Sar, S., Martin, J. D., & Moultrie, J. L. (2020). Binge-Watching Serial Video Content: Exploring the Subjective Phenomenology of the Binge-Watching Experience. Mass Communication and Society, 24(1), 130-154.
sources.claim: Documents the gap at the centre of this entry as a measured thing rather than an impression: the parasocial scale items used include 'I miss my favorite characters when the show is on break between seasons', and the paper notes these bonds form in proportion to time spent with the characters. That is the missing-slot effect the summary describes - the thing a continuous feed removes is not the intensity but the absence. Publisher returns 403 to an unauthenticated request; bibliographic record confirmed against Crossref.

entries.title: A mob is a parasocial event
entries.summary: Framing online harassment as a mob, and asking who is on it.
entries.significance: The most useful analytical frame available for a behaviour with no consequences for the people committing it, and the phrase that gets people to ask the question at all.

sources.claim: THE PAPER'S OWN FRAMING IS THIS ENTRY. 'After an accusation of wrongdoing, an outrage mob appears. Initially, just a few condemn the accused. But before long, more and more people pile on, hastily meting out punishment with little regard for evidence or opposing perspectives.' Four studies, n=10,343
sources.citation: Kteily, N., & Jordan, J. How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking.

sources.claim: AND THE FINDING THAT CUTS AGAINST THE MORAL READING: there is NO reputational reward for not looking. Non-lookers were rated more loyal to the cause, but that was outweighed by a larger hit to perceived competence and fairness - evaluators rewarded punishers who LOOKED more generously
sources.citation: Kteily & Jordan, How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking.

sources.claim: The mechanism, named by the people in it: 'brigading, dogpiling, or calling out'. Amplification is the trigger - content moral-outrage spreads faster within like-minded networks, and 'drama' is consumed as entertainment in front of an audience
sources.citation: Marwick, A. E. (2021). Morally Motivated Networked Harassment as Normative Reinforcement. Social Media Society, 7(2).

sources.claim: What it actually achieves: harassment frequently results in the ACCUSED SELF-CENSORING, so the pile-on functions as a regulating force that removes speech from the public sphere. Neither platforms nor legal regulation protects against it. Interviews with 28 targets and 9 Trust and Safety workers
sources.citation: Marwick, A. E. (2021). Social Media Society, 7(2).

sources.claim: Not a partisan tactic, which is the part usually left out: this is used across the ideological spectrum, and the amplification runs in both directions depending on which network node shares it
sources.citation: Marwick, A. E. (2021), Social Media Society, 7(2).

sources.claim: WHY IT ESCALATES: analysis of 231 threads finds networked harassment runs in three phases - target introduction, network decision, network response - and that the crowd added narrative elements in at least 80% of threads, producing Continuous Narrative Escalation. The crowd is not reacting to the story. It is writing it
sources.citation: Stoking the Flames: Understanding Escalation in an Online Harassment Community. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (2024).

sources.claim: AND THE PART THAT MADE ME STOP: takedown requests are misused by the community and repurposed as ELEMENTS TO FURTHER FUEL THE NARRATIVE. Reporting abuse is itself harvested as content
sources.citation: Stoking the Flames: Understanding Escalation in an Online Harassment Community (ACM CSCW 2024), analysis of 100 takedown request threads.

entries.title: The assistant arrives
entries.summary: A voice assistant on every phone, addressing the user by name, knowing the user's calendar, and present in the home.
entries.significance: The crossover entry point. The assistant is not a celebrity and is not a friend, but it is a presence that knows you, and the relationship forms anyway and is categorised as neither friendship nor tool use.

sources.claim: THE TITLE OF THE PAPER IS A PARTICIPANT'S SENTENCE. The study is titled 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine' after a subject's own private Instagram post about the conversational agent Lee. The authors state they did not expect any participant to develop a personal attachment
sources.citation: Yu, Q., Nguyen, T., Prakkamakul, S., & Salehi, N. 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine': Speaking with Computers Affects Self-disclosure (UC Berkeley, X Lab).

sources.claim: The mechanism, measured: people skipped FEWER invasive questions when listening and speaking than when reading and typing. It is the combination of both, not either alone, that triggers the social-actor response. The authors flag this as a new factor in user privacy concerns
sources.citation: Yu, Nguyen, Prakkamakul & Salehi, 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine'.

sources.claim: The warmth channel is where the work happens: emotional and opinion-based self-disclosure significantly increased perceived warmth over both normal conversation and factual disclosure, and high-intimacy disclosure fostered closer psychological connection, perceived empathy, friendliness and trustworthiness
sources.citation: Sun, X., Shen, T., Jiang, Q., & Jiang, B. (2025). Research on the Impact of an AI Voice Assistant's Gender and Self-Disclosure Strategies.

sources.claim: And why disclosure strategy has to be chosen rather than defaulted: research finds users who perceive an assistant as human-like form greater intimacy from PERSONAL disclosure, while users who perceive it as a machine form it from FACTUAL disclosure. The same utterance works only if you have already been read as a person
sources.citation: Sun et al. (2025), citing Saffarizadeh et al. (2024).

sources.claim: Gender is a dial on the conduit, not a decoration: a randomized experiment with 120 participants found a female voice produces higher perceived ANTHROPOMORPHISM, which in turn raises the credibility of the information it gives. Female voices also raised intended self-disclosure
sources.citation: Do People Trust Female more than Male as a Voice Assistant? (Tampere University).

sources.claim: The honest counterweight: warmth is the cheap channel and competence is not. Fiske et al. (2006) hold that warmth is the primary dimension while competence requires substantially more evidence to change - and disclosure strategy moved warmth but NOT competence. Reciprocal self-disclosure can also backfire entirely when users suspect manipulation, producing loss of trust, service cessation, and false answers in future disclosures
sources.citation: Sun et al. (2025), citing Fiske et al. (2006) and Collins & Miller (1994).

entries.title: Justin.tv becomes Twitch
entries.summary: Streaming gets a category, a vocabulary, a schedule, and a professional class of people who stream full time.
entries.significance: The first platform to treat a live one-sided relationship as a category worth designing for deliberately rather than tolerating incidentally.

sources.claim: Twitch launched 6 June 2011 as a spin-off of Justin.tv's gaming section, named for 'twitch gameplay', in public beta
sources.citation: Twitch (service). Wikipedia, citing contemporary coverage.

sources.claim: The founder's own account of how a parasocial bond was accidentally engineered: an audio idea became a 24/7 camera feed following one person, then chat, then a community around watching
sources.citation: Kan, J. (2011). Why Starting Justin.tv Was A Really Bad Idea, But I'm Glad We Did It Anyway. TechCrunch (guest post).

sources.claim: Justin.tv began as Justin Kan broadcasting his life 24/7 from a cap-mounted camera at midnight on 19 March 2007 - the first and most parasocial thing on the platform
sources.citation: Justin.tv. Wikipedia.

sources.claim: Intimacy turned to intrusion almost immediately: viewers swatted Kan and sent large delivery orders to his apartment
sources.citation: Justin.tv. Wikipedia, citing AllThingsD coverage of the TwitchTV launch.

sources.claim: Contemporary launch coverage, 6 June 2011, E3 unveiling
sources.citation: Duryee, T. (2011). Justin.tv Broadcasts Gamers' Every Move on TwitchTV. AllThingsD.

entries.title: Fandom wars
entries.summary: Organised conflict between fanbases, with brigading, ratioing and coalition behaviour, conducted with the grammar of war.
entries.significance: Fan organisations developed the same apparatus as states: recruitment, propaganda, alliance, denial. And the participants believe they are defending art.

sources.claim: Documented case: the #fakewesteros Twitter community during the final season of Game of Thrones - fans of a character declared dead fighting fans who knew otherwise, over leaks
sources.citation: Forcier, E. (2019). When the world ends: Study of #fakewesteros twitter fan community during the final season of Game of Thrones. Proceedings of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 56(1), 654-655.

sources.claim: Fanwars are named by the fans themselves as the reason their own space is toxic - some avoid the app or deactivate their accounts rather than stay
sources.citation: Ascue et al., Annyeong, Saranghae (De La Salle University).

entries.title: Swatting
entries.summary: Sending a false emergency report to a real address to provoke an armed police response, because of a grievance about a streamer.
entries.significance: The final boundary. A parasocial grievance aimed at a public figure lands on an innocent third party with a weapon, and no amount of the bond being sincere changes the outcome for the person who is shot.

sources.claim: The term was coined in 2011 and the practice escalated from pranks to lethal: a 60-year-old man was killed in a swatting in California in 2013, after which California enacted specific anti-swattiing legislation. Armed police are dispatched as a joke with someone else's address attached
sources.citation: Swatting (Wikipedia).

entries.title: Gamergate
entries.summary: Coordinated harassment of women in games, disguised as a debate about whether harassment should be allowed.
entries.significance: The case study for how a parasocial grievance gets weaponised: people who felt strongly about a hobby organised against individuals who had done nothing personal to them. The counter is to ask who benefits from the fight, not what the disagreement is about.

sources.claim: August 2014: a campaign targeting women in games, organised largely through an anonymous account, escalating within days to coordinated harassment, doxxing and death threats. The FBI investigated. Wikipedia's article is the de facto record and its revision history is itself an artifact of the harassment
sources.citation: GamerGate (Wikipedia).

sources.claim: The essay that started it was about the emotional labour of game design, which the campaign reframed as a grievance about women
sources.citation: GamerGate (Wikipedia), discussing Begum Bayrak's 'Depression Quest' and Zoe Quinn.

entries.title: The podcast as an intimate medium
entries.summary: A voice in your ear, unedited, twice a week, for years. The most parasocial habit in the English language and rarely discussed as such.
entries.significance: Nobody wears a costume and nobody mentions the format, so it never got examined. Researchers eventually measured it and found listeners score high on exactly the traits predicted: novelty-seeking, curiosity, and a need for good conversation.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Pedestrian.tv, 2026

entries.title: Parasocial research on creators begins
entries.summary: A wave of studies measuring parasocial relationships with YouTubers, livestreamers and vloggers rather than with television hosts.
entries.significance: The literature caught up with the medium about a decade late, and then discovered that the newer bonds are not the same shape. Livestreamers can see the room. That changes the theory, not just the population.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Gerrath & Usrey, 2014

entries.title: The failing endorsement
entries.summary: Evidence that the value of a celebrity endorsement falls when the audience suspects the relationship is a transaction.
entries.significance: The parasocial bond is doing the work, which means the suspicion destroys the asset. This is why an advert that says 'I love this' from somebody you follow is worth less than the same advert from a stranger: the transaction has to stay invisible.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: de Vries & Gilovich, 2015

entries.title: The people who are supposed to be reachable
entries.summary: Attachment to somebody we are not supposed to have feelings about: the teacher, the landlord, the local news anchor, the doctor's receptionist, the AI assistant that has read everything typed. The category no fandom site will admit exists.
entries.significance: The one that proves this is a hub rather than a fan site. The bond is identical in shape to the one with a celebrity and completely different in power, because here the other person does not know they are being related to and may have very little power to say no. It is also where my own classroom is, which is why it is an section and not a footnote.

sources.claim: THE CATEGORY NO FANDOM SITE WILL ADMIT TO, demonstrated in a controlled experiment on people who were not asked to develop an attachment: one did, and said so publicly about the agent. Attachment to a machine is not a subculture. It is the default failure mode
sources.citation: Yu, Nguyen, Prakkamakul & Salehi, 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine' (UC Berkeley, X Lab).

sources.claim: Scale of what gets volunteered: on average participants skipped only 3 of 21 closeness-generating questions, responses were honest and conversational, most disclosed family life and values, some shared sensitive information, and one answered a question about their greatest accomplishment with 'Recovering from my mental illness'
sources.citation: Yu, Nguyen, Prakkamakul & Salehi, 'I Almost Fell in Love with a Machine'.

sources.claim: The category with the clearest evidence of failure: a real institution with a real constituency, using the full influencer apparatus, still cannot produce reciprocity. Priests seldom reply. The tie stays one-sided
sources.citation: Between pulpit and platform: Parasocial bonds in Filipino priests' social media ministry (2025).

sources.claim: And a counter-intuitive mechanism worth having: expressing positive feelings was the technique secular influencers rely on and the priests omitted, and the harvest step changed with it
sources.citation: Witzel, The Cultivation and Harvesting of Parasocial Relationships for Evangelism.

entries.title: The free trial
entries.summary: A relationship with a competitor offered free while a subscription relationship is locked in behind the same login.
entries.significance: Platforms discovered that a user will defend the platform they have a relationship with against the platform offering them a better deal. The parasocial bond is now a competitive moat, and it is documented as such in the filings.

sources.claim: The free trial as a documented pattern rather than an anecdote: Hidden Subscription is defined as charging a recurring fee under the pretense of a one-time fee or a free trial, and users often learn of it only days or months later
sources.citation: Mathur, A., Acar, G., Friedman, M. J., Lucherini, E., Mayer, J., Chetty, M., & Narayanan, A. (2019). Dark Patterns at Scale. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 3(CSCW), Article 81.

sources.claim: And it is paired with a barrier on the way out: the same paper finds Hidden Subscription frequently co-occurs with Hard to Cancel, making the recurring charge harder to end than it was to begin
sources.citation: Mathur et al. (2019).

entries.title: Live chat, two-way
entries.summary: A live stream with a visible comment feed, where the creator can read the room while the room watches itself. The first mass parasocial environment where the one-sided bond visibly, continuously, acknowledges you.
entries.significance: It solved a problem nobody had been able to solve: making the one-sided bond feel reciprocal without the labour of a real relationship. A creator glancing at your comment costs them nothing and lands like recognition. It is also the exact mechanism monetised two years later by the gifting economy.

sources.claim: THE SITE'S THESIS, PUBLISHED: live streaming moves the parasocial relationship from one-sided to 'one-and-a-half sided', characterised by the potential for reciprocal communication, community affiliation and presence. Peer-reviewed, in a journal
sources.citation: The one-and-a-half sided parasocial relationship. Current Opinion in Psychology.

sources.claim: The bond persists through non-reciprocity: users keep following favourites despite failing to get a response - which is the whole subject, measured
sources.citation: Crawford et al. (2020), cited in The one-and-a-half sided parasocial relationship.

sources.claim: Merely WITNESSING the figure interact with other community members reinforces the viewer's connection - the bond forms on other people's exchanges, not on your own
sources.citation: Stever & Lawson (2013), cited in The one-and-a-half sided parasocial relationship.

sources.claim: Measured in the chat itself: streamer-targeted messages carry greater verbal immediacy than viewer-targeted ones (M=-1.13 vs M=-2.06, t(4763)=-49.74, p<.001, d=.72), with 'we' for 'you' as the marker. Viewers address the streamer as a peer
sources.citation: Parasocial cues: The ubiquity of parasocial relationships on Twitch (2021).

sources.claim: Survey evidence: every interaction feature tested correlated significantly with parasocial scores, chat strongest (r(116)=.611), follow weakest (r=.194). Higher loneliness and longer relationships predicted stronger PSRs
sources.citation: Correlations between Twitch's interaction features and parasocial relationships and streamer influence (Regelbrugge, 2024).

entries.title: Parasocial persuasion
entries.summary: Using a one-sided bond to move somebody: the celebrity endorsement, the fan club vote, the ad that works because the viewer already feels known. And the finding that ads featuring attractive models can actively reduce purchase intention in people who feel excluded.
entries.significance: The double-edged result is the interesting part. The same mechanism that makes somebody buy the product can make them not buy it, purely as a function of whether they felt the ad was addressed to them. Persuasion runs through recognition, not through liking.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: de Vries, L., & Gilovich, T. (2015). Title and venue not yet recorded.

entries.title: The ratio
entries.summary: A mass coordinated response in which the metric being weaponised is attention rather than truth.
entries.significance: A parasocial bond turned into a weapon against a public figure, fired by people who are not the target and derive nothing but participation. It is a crowd acting out a parasocial relationship with a stranger who did not know it was happening.

entries.title: The subscription tier
entries.summary: A monthly payment that buys recognition, and a chat in which the size of that payment is the mechanism for being noticed. Gifting, tiers, emotes, raids.
entries.significance: It solved the problem nobody had been able to solve: making a one-sided bond feel reciprocal without the labour of an actual relationship. A glance at your comment costs the creator nothing and lands like recognition. It also means the amount of money is now the amount of personhood, which is a strange thing to be true about somebody's evening.

sources.claim: At scale: 868,940 users across 59 channels. Co-interactive behaviour between USERS has a stronger effect on willingness to subscribe than passive or active behaviour, and one user's reciprocated interaction raises other users' willingness to subscribe. The one-and-a-half sidedness, monetised
sources.citation: Brundl, S., Matt, C., Hess, T., & Engert, S. (2023). How synchronous participation affects the willingness to subscribe to social live streaming services. European Journal of Information Systems, 32(5), 800-817.

entries.title: Who holds the dream
