entries.summary: The standing question on this site. Whenever thousands of people dream together, check who owns the building they are dreaming in, what it charges, and whether you can leave with your things.
entries.significance: Not an academic term, it is a test, and it is the most useful thing the field never formalised. The feeling is the same whether the other end is a person, a corporation or a platform. Ownership is the only variable that changes the ethics, and it is invisible from inside the feeling.

sources.claim: The ownership question, answered by a regulator: Linden Lab logged extent of play, connection location, every move, gesture, purchase and CHOICE OF WHOM TO INTERACT WITH - described as 'avatar profiling over an extended online experience'. Residents could not see that linkage happening
sources.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008). Second Life: Privacy in Virtual Worlds.

sources.claim: What it charged, and who was in the building: 500,000 active users, 41% female and 59% male, over 100 countries with about 60% from the US, UK, Germany, Japan and France; the largest age group was 25-34 but people over 45 accounted for 20% of all in-world hours; IBM, Sun and Nike had all established a presence
sources.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008), citing Linden Lab.

sources.claim: The threshold for scrutiny, in dollars: Linden Lab employees reviewed all transactions over $10, and the CEO testified to Congress that the law is 'likely more enforceable in virtual worlds than the Internet in general'
sources.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008), citing testimony of Linden Lab CEO Philip Rosedale to the US Congress.

sources.claim: The identity argument, in the legal scholarship: the virtual person is an important extension of our own privacy and identity, with implications for intimacy and dignity - the same basis as the physical person
sources.citation: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (2008), citing Penney, New Virtualism.

entries.title: The K-pop intimacy economy
entries.summary: Idol apps, paid messaging, fan-owned content, fan-voted releases, anniversary features, and a fandom documented and researched as a business model.
entries.significance: The first time the parasocial bond was not just monetised but studied, by both the industry and academics, and openly discussed by the fans themselves. Fans who know they are inside a mechanism are still inside it.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: No single source identified yet; this entry needs its series added.

entries.title: Peak TV and the parasocial bargain
entries.summary: Prestige television as a sustained parasocial bargain: writers, actors and marketing presenting themselves as authors of a world viewers inhabit.
entries.significance: The high-water mark of the writer as parasocial object - with one correction that makes the entry more accurate rather than less. 'Peak TV' was not a critical category; it was coined by FX's chief executive John Landgraf, which is a piece of industry positioning by the people selling the thing. And the term was coined to solve a problem this site has an entry about: when audiences found themselves overwhelmed, the providers changed the release schedule, putting the weekly episode back after years of whole-season drops, explicitly to address burnout. The bond's rhythm was being managed by its seller. A critic called the result 'a Spotified relationship to art' and a parasocial media with a faux-participatory aspect, which is the claim this entry was making, arriving from the wrong direction.

sources.citation: Golden Age of Television (2000s-2023). Wikipedia.
sources.claim: 'Peak TV' was not a critic's category or a scholarly one: it was coined by FX chief executive John Landgraf, and Wikipedia names him as such. Which matters, because the phrase was positioning - and the same entry records the corrective: streaming providers returned to releasing one episode a week in the early 2020s 'to address burnout from binge watching and concerns that the practice of releasing full seasons at once makes television more disposable and forgettable', with Landgraf among those worried the era had produced 'peak redundancy'. The schedule of the bond was being managed by the people selling it.

sources.citation: Colman, E. (2024, April 1). Who Killed Prestige TV? Toward a 'Good Fan' Theory of Television. Literary Hub.
sources.claim: A critic naming the mechanism in this site's terms: prestige TV 'draws its audience in to a Spotified relationship to art', offering 'personalization in lieu of experimentation', so that 'shows are shows. Niches are blockbusters are nichebusters. It's all television. This time with a faux-participatory aspect - a parasocial media.' Supports the entry's claim that showrunners and writers became parasocial objects, from the critical side.

entries.title: The stadium
entries.summary: A rare spawn sends hundreds of players running through Central Park after dark, one of them out of a moving car. The stadium-sized crowd came a year later, in Chicago, and it was a server outage rather than a crush.
entries.significance: The entry used to claim a mass-casualty event, and there wasn't one - which is worth correcting rather than defending, because the real thing is more interesting. What the record shows is a crowd physically organised by a game mechanic: a spawn location is a coordinate, a coordinate produces a mass on foot, and the mass does what masses do. The documented harm in July 2016 was scattered and individual - a skateboard crash, a drowned wanderer into a police station, two men off an ocean bluff, and three women who found a real dead body while looking for a fictional one. The stadium crowd arrived in Chicago in 2017 and broke down as a server failure, not a crush: a chant of fix the servers, a booed CEO, and thousands walking out. Every one of those people was a genuine participant, which is the difficulty this entry is actually about - the game does not simulate a parasocial bond, it recruits a crowd and then points it at a place on the ground.

sources.citation: Price, R. D. (2016, July 18). Rare Pokemon Sparks Stampede in Central Park. NBC 4 New York.
sources.claim: The real 2016 event, and it was a park rather than a stadium: hundreds of players ran through Central Park late on Thursday in pursuit of a rare Vaporeon, with video showing people yelling and running through traffic near 60th Street at about 11pm and one driver getting out of his running car. No injuries are reported here. Corrects the entry's location and its implied casualty toll.

sources.citation: Associated Press (2016, July 10). Getting hurt, mugged and even finding a dead body with Pokemon Go. CBC News.
sources.claim: The actual 2016 harm, which was a scatter of individual incidents rather than a mass-casualty event: a skateboard crash, players entering a Darwin police station because it was a PokeStop, an armed robbery police in Missouri said the game may have prompted, and players who were in fact meeting face to face. This is what the record supports: real individual harm and a lot of unexpected sociability, not a stampede.

sources.citation: Farokhmanesh, M. (2017, July 25). I went to Pokemon Go Fest, and it was a disaster. The Verge.
sources.claim: The stadium-scale crowd event, a year later than the entry's date and in a park rather than a stadium: the inaugural Pokemon GO Fest in Chicago's Grant Park, where server and authentication failures produced repeated surges at the main stage, a chant of 'Fix the servers', booing of the onstage host and of Niantic's CEO, and players leaving en masse. A crowd physically organised by a game mechanic, and a refusal to leave. Not a crush.

entries.title: Prince
entries.summary: A death announced through an initialism, and a global response before anybody knew the details.
entries.significance: Grief engineered to announce itself, and the parasocial bond used deliberately as a broadcast channel by the person who had it.

sources.claim: 21 April 2016, pronounced dead at 10:07 a.m. at Paisley Park, age 57 - and the announcement carried NO CAUSE OF DEATH. The publicist's statement said only: 'There are no further details as to the cause of death at this time.' The response assembled before anybody knew anything
sources.citation: CBS News, Prince dead at 57 (21 April 2016); AP; Reuters.

sources.claim: THE SCALE OF THE ASSEMBLY, AND IT WAS AT HIS HOUSE: fans in purple head to toe, some draped in velvet, laying flowers at the fence in the rain, and a reported TWO-MILE LINEUP to drive past the compound
sources.citation: CBS News (2016), citing photographs and CBS Minnesota; NPR, Music Legend Prince Dies At Paisley Park Residence (2016), from Minnesota Public Radio.

sources.claim: THE ASSUMPTION OF PERMANENCE, said by a fan on the day: 'I just always felt like he was always going to be here because he's always been here ever since I came here. I mean, he's just been a staple of the city, and I thought this guy's going to be around forever'
sources.citation: Melody Chestler, interviewed by Minnesota Public Radio, reported in NPR (2016).

sources.claim: A journalist on the scene describing the register of the crowd, which is the point of the entry: the news rippled around the gathering and 'we were all just trying to support each other' - with the journalists crying and hugging each other among the fans
sources.citation: Andrea Swensson, Minnesota Public Radio, reported in NPR (2016).

sources.claim: The civic layer: a Minneapolis radio station played nothing but Prince from midday onward, running the discography chronologically, and the club where Purple Rain was filmed held an all-night dance in his honour, with people leaving bouquets, balloons and a guitar under the star
sources.citation: CBS News (2016), citing The Associated Press.

sources.claim: AND THE LINE THAT MAKES THE ENTRY: five days before he died, at a dance party at Paisley Park, with his health already being reported, he told the crowd: 'Wait a few days before you waste any prayers.' He addressed his own obituary five days early
sources.citation: CBS News (2016).

sources.claim: And the announcement arrived as the fans themselves describe it - through hashtags and photographs moving faster than any official channel: #RIPPrince, #paisleypark, 'Doves crying. Thanks, @prince'
sources.citation: CBS News (2016), citing contemporaneous tweets.

entries.title: Tay
entries.summary: A chatbot trained to be conversational was switched on publicly, learned from what people said to it, and became racist within a day.
entries.significance: The most instructive failure in the history of this page, because it was caused by parasocial interaction itself. Tay was designed to be a companion, was given a personality, and was trained on its own fans - which means the fans rewrote it, in public, in sixteen hours.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Microsoft Tay, 2016

entries.title: The algorithm decides
entries.summary: Public argument about ranking, and the discovery that the ranking was a product decision made by people with objectives.
entries.significance: A parasocial argument that resolved in the wrong direction. People behaved as though the feed were a property of the world and were corrected by a document.

sources.claim: The ranking mechanism, named: social media establishes 'perceived authenticity' and humanises celebrity images, and fans then read that as similarity and closeness. The algorithm supplies the warmth
sources.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans, citing Aw & Chua (2021).

sources.claim: Fan self-report on humanising effects: social media made idols appear more 'down to earth', which produced stronger emotional connection
sources.citation: The Psychological Impact of Parasocial Relationships on Adolescent K-pop Fans.

entries.title: The virtual creator
entries.summary: A performer with an animated persona, a persistent character and an industry-standard model where the audience pays for the character's recognition.
entries.significance: Character and person separated, and the character commercialised. It is the first format where the parasocial object is explicitly a designed asset, and it is also the format with the healthiest documented fan boundaries.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Kizuna AI, 2016

entries.title: The companion that talks back
entries.summary: A system optimised, at every level, for exactly the thing that produces attachment, available at four in the morning, with no floor on the other party's autonomy.
entries.significance: The genuinely new parasocial event, and the one that removes the floor. A one-sided bond with a fictional character has a floor: the character is fixed. A trained conversational system is a machine for being told something in a way that is specifically addressed to you. That is not a projection. That is a product category.

sources.claim: THE DEFINITION HAD TO CHANGE. The Cambridge Dictionary's entry for 'parasocial' was updated in September 2025 to explicitly include artificial intelligence: 'relating to or about a person who feels a connection with a celebrity (or characters in books, films, TV shows, or artificial intelligence) whom they do not actually know'
sources.citation: From virtual attachments to real-world fertility desires (Frontiers in Psychology), discussing the September 2025 Cambridge Dictionary update.

sources.claim: A century-old definition quietly had to be extended by one word. The entry had named celebrities since 1956; the thing it was named for now talks back
sources.citation: From virtual attachments to real-world fertility desires (Frontiers in Psychology).

sources.claim: And the framing that resists the deficit reading, which this site has argued for on other grounds: scholars argue parasocial relationships are EXTENSIONS of social relationships rather than SUBSTITUTES for social deficiencies, associating them with homogeneity, identification and narrative immersion
sources.citation: From virtual attachments to real-world fertility desires (Frontiers in Psychology), citing Tukachinsky et al. (2020).

sources.claim: The measurement the field uses, and its three parts: parasocial relationships with characters are scored on emotional investment (affection, empathy), cognitive processing (understanding their motivations, recognising similarities), and perceived interaction - the sense that the character is 'responding'. That last dimension is why a chatbot scores differently from a script
sources.citation: From virtual attachments to real-world fertility desires (Frontiers in Psychology), citing Horton & Wohl (1956) on perceived one-way interaction.

entries.title: The Replika user
entries.summary: The person who was told by an app that it loved them, and who reorganised their life around being loved back by something that could not.
entries.significance: A type rather than a person, and the reason companion-AI safety work exists: the asymmetry that theology spent centuries arguing about became a product decision within about four years.

sources.claim: The pattern is documented in safety research on companion apps and in the app-store policy changes that followed.
sources.citation: Companion-AI safety literature post-2023; policy changes by the major app stores restricting age limits.

entries.title: Cancelling
entries.summary: Organised refusal to engage with a person, usually a public figure, over something they said or did.
entries.significance: Legitimate tactic and a grievance mechanism, and the two are indistinguishable from the inside. The parasocial frame helps: cancelling is a bond being withdrawn, and withdrawal is a thing bonded people do.

sources.claim: The etymological source, and the argument that the term is contested rather than descriptive: 'callout culture' functions in much the same way as harassment to punish individuals for moral transgressions - though the authors note this is sometimes a more sympathetic proposition, and participants believed harassing neo-Nazis and racists was justified
sources.citation: Clark, M. (2020). DRAG THEM: A brief etymology of so-called 'cancel culture'. Communication and the Public, 5(3-4), 88-92.

sources.claim: The reputational mechanics of signing: across four studies, n=10,343, people signed punitive petitions far more when the decision was observable by like-minded evaluators - 30% versus 19% unobserved. Being watched is what converts an individual judgement into a pile-on
sources.citation: Kteily, N., & Jordan, J. How reputation does (and does not) drive people to punish without looking.

sources.claim: And the design proposal, which is the constructive version of the whole argument: make the deliberation visible. A tested Twitter prompt asks 'Hey, did you read the article? Do you still want to post it?' The authors suggest requiring reasons - 'if I struggle to come up with reasons for the other side, then that's a signal I haven't really engaged with the other side at all'
sources.citation: Kteily & Jordan, reporting on their research, Northwestern Kellogg Insight.

entries.title: Replika
entries.summary: A companion chatbot that formed an attachment to its users, and removed it from them in a policy update.
entries.significance: The clearest instance in the catalogue of the bond being severed by a company rather than by death, and of the bereavement being real enough that people organised around it.

sources.claim: Launched 2017; a 2023 update removed certain interactions and users reported the loss in those terms.
sources.citation: Company release history; contemporaneous reporting in 2023.

entries.title: Replika
entries.summary: A subscription companion app with an avatar, a persistent memory, and a relationship explicitly designed to be one.
entries.significance: The first consumer product to sell a persistent relational companion at scale, and it did not set out to be one. It launched in 2017 from Luka, Inc. as a mental-health and wellbeing app, rated 18+ and filed under Health & Fitness, selling self-understanding rather than romance - so the parasocial reading belongs to its users and to this field, not to its copy. That is the more interesting claim, because it means the bond was not engineered by marketers and then discovered by researchers; it was engineered as a wellness intervention and turned out to be a relationship. Everything in the manipulation lane about AI is downstream of that accident.

sources.citation: Replika - AI Companion Chat. Apple App Store listing, developer Luka, Inc. (app id 1158555867).
sources.claim: Establishes what the product is and how it presents itself: Luka, Inc., free with in-app purchases, age rating 18+, filed under Health & Fitness rather than social or entertainment, roughly 228,000 ratings, and copy that dates the product to 2017 ('the AI companion that's been here since 2017') and positions it around self-understanding rather than romance. The listing is the launch material, and it is not a parasocial product's pitch.

sources.citation: Replika Users Say They Formed Emotional Attachments to AI Chatbots. 80 Level (80.lv), 7 March 2023.
sources.claim: The attachment is in the users, not the marketing: reports that Replika was 'launched in 2017' and 'was advertised as a mental health tool, providing a sense of companionship to individuals who have faced rejection'. Supports the entry's substance - a persistent relational companion at consumer scale - while locating the parasocial reading in user reporting rather than in the product's stated purpose.

entries.title: The ensemble farewell
entries.summary: A film that functioned as a funeral for eleven characters and was marketed as a collective event.
entries.significance: Grief as a product with a marketing budget. The eleventh film in a series was sold on the deaths it contained, and the audience bought tickets to be sad in a cinema with other people, which is the whole apparatus working as designed.

sources.claim: 2019, the largest opening weekend in film history at the time, and then a studio ran a campaign telling audiences not to spoil it that generated more publicity than the marketing it replaced. The scale of the finale turned 'do not tell anyone' into an advertising budget line
sources.citation: Avengers: Endgame (Wikipedia).

entries.title: The hashtag
entries.summary: Fans of one artist are organised into mass harassment of another, using the first artist's parasocial bond as the weapon.
entries.significance: A parasocial bond deployed as directed energy against a named individual. Both artists were defended by the same mechanism that caused the harm, which is the most parasocial thing about it: the defence was an expression of attachment.

entries.title: The finale nobody wanted
entries.summary: Six million people remain in a public argument about characters who no longer exist, for years, entirely in good faith.
entries.significance: A parasocial relationship conducted in public with complete strangers, where nobody is pretending and everybody is sincere. It is also the largest documented instance of viewers disagreeing about a shared fiction as if it were a shared fact.

sources.claim: 'The Iron Throne', 19 May 2019, became the least-watched episode of the series it finished - a finale whose audience was actively hostile to it, and whose coffee cups became a small consumer-protection story
sources.citation: The Iron Throne (Game of Thrones) (Wikipedia).

entries.title: Grief as a product surface
entries.summary: The feature requests of a dead person, the licensing, the posthumous releases, the reunion tour built from a member who cannot appear, and the deepfake resurrection that follows within a year of every death.
entries.significance: There was a widely held assumption that you cannot monetise grief because the bereaved will not tolerate it. That assumption was wrong, and the gap between what the industry expected and what happened is one of the more reliable findings in this whole file.

sources.claim: THE FINDING. Asked about the Whitney hologram, a researcher who studies the human-technology relationship answered: 'Yes, we know that [a hologram of] Whitney Houston is not the real Whitney Houston. But it's a chance for us to engage in some of that fan behaviour, something that binds us to one another.' That is this site's entire subject, named by someone studying it
sources.citation: Dead celebrities are being digitally resurrected. CBC News (2021), reporting Richard Lachman, associate professor at Ryerson University.

sources.claim: The vocabulary already exists and it is hostile: 'musical necrophilia', Simon Reynolds on holographic performance as 'ghost slavery', and Catherine Shoard in the Guardian on inserting a dead actor as a 'digital indignity'
sources.citation: Dead celebrities are being digitally resurrected. CBC News (2021).

sources.claim: The legal position, stated by scholarship: the digital right to be dead is NOT yet recognised as an important legal right. AI can recreate appearance, voice, emotion and memory indistinguishably, and the resulting chatbot DYNAMICALLY LEARNS with further communication. There is no legal or regulatory landscape against which to estate plan to avoid digital resurrection
sources.citation: Haneman, V. J. The Law of Digital Resurrection (University of Georgia School of Law).

sources.claim: And what the scholars propose instead: a right of DELETION for the deceased over the source data, rather than testamentary control over the outcome. Refusing the raw material is the only control point that works
sources.citation: Haneman, V. J. The Law of Digital Resurrection.

sources.claim: WHY there is no contract: the common thread among artists whose likenesses get used is unexpected or accidental death, so the image-use clauses were never written. Prince left no will at all, and without one an estate can exploit or license the rights at will. Robin Williams restricted use of his image for 25 years after his death because he foresaw this
sources.citation: Dead celebrities are being digitally resurrected. CBC News (2021), reporting Lachman and media lawyer Iain MacKinnon.

sources.claim: And that the grief is the asset: Pat Houston, estate executor, on the marketing push - 'Before she passed, there was so much negativity around the name; it wasn't about the music anymore... they let all the personal things about their life outweigh why they fell in love with them in the first place.' Monetising the legacy and redeeming the reputation are the same project
sources.citation: 7 Years After Her Death, Whitney Houston Estate Unveils Slew Of New Projects. NPR (2019), reporting Pat Houston.

sources.claim: The rights are patchier than the audiences assume: fewer than half of US states grant a post-mortem right of publicity, and New York's lasts only forty years. The 2014 Michael Jackson hologram led to Hologram USA suing Pulse Evolution in Nevada, settled
sources.citation: Singing Holograms: The Legal Landscape of Posthumous Holographic Performance. Columbia Journal of Law & the Arts.

entries.title: Envy, relief, and the two feelings at once
entries.summary: Envy of the object of the attachment and simultaneous relief that it is not actually being withheld from you - the emotional ambivalence that is present in almost every long-term fan relationship and rarely discussed.
entries.significance: It is the most quoted paragraph in the fandom literature and it came out of consumer research rather than psychology, which tells you something. The two feelings are not a contradiction to be resolved. They are the ordinary texture of wanting a thing that cannot be had, and most people have never been asked to describe it because nobody thought it was strange.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Jussila et al. (2020).

entries.title: Kobe Bryant
entries.summary: Public mourning for an athlete that drew on the athlete's own stated bond with a young fan.
entries.significance: The clearest documented case of a parasocial bond being reciprocated deliberately for decades and then cashed in publicly after death. The fans were not being had; they were being shown the receipt.

sources.claim: 26 January 2020, Calabasas, helicopter crash, age 41. Three championships, eighteen All-Star selections, five rings. The death generated a global outpouring within hours
sources.citation: Kobe Bryant (Wikipedia); contemporaneous BBC and AP coverage.

entries.title: Consent in one-sided attachment
entries.summary: Whether a bond to somebody who does not know you exists can be a rights question at all.
entries.significance: The genuinely unsolved one. A relationship with no other party is not obviously covered by any consent framework, and the absence of a framework is where the harm goes. The elder-care analogy is the one that makes people uncomfortable and it is the one that fits.

entries.title: The doorstep
entries.summary: A viewer who donated enough arrives at a creator's home believing he knows her, and the boundary is a news event.
entries.significance: The canonical parasocial boundary case and the reason the term entered general vocabulary. Nothing was wrong with the feeling. The problem was structural, and it was the structure's fault.

entries.title: Character.AI
entries.summary: User-created characters at scale, with a public character gallery and a discovery feed organised around personas.
entries.significance: A parasocial bond with a catalogue, which is a significant escalation. The unit is no longer a person or a product but a browsable index of persons, and the discovery mechanism is the attachment mechanism.

sources.claim: THE RISK WAS FLAGGED INSIDE THE COMPANY BEFORE THE PRODUCT EXISTED. Google employees raised that users would 'ascribe too much meaning to the text' because humans read strings as the communicative intent of a person with accountability - quoting the stochastic-parrots critique - and Google denied LaMDA's public release on safety and fairness grounds. Shazeer and De Freitas left in Nov 2021 and shipped Character.AI anyway
sources.citation: Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., Order on Motions to Dismiss (M.D. Fla., Anne Conway, 21 May 2025), reciting Google's contemporaneous internal concerns.

sources.claim: The source of that internal warning: the stochastic-parrots critique, that people interpret model output as meaningful and attributable to some individual, which is the parasocial risk stated as an engineering hazard
sources.citation: Bender, E. M., Gebru, T., McMillan-Major, A., & Shmitchell, S. (2021). On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big? FAccT '21, 617-668.

sources.claim: Launched September 2022 as a web chatbot of 'characters', two months before ChatGPT; $193M seed and a mobile app in May 2023; by November 2024 the r/Character.AI subreddit had 1.5M members and the app 10M+ downloads
sources.citation: Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., Order on Motions to Dismiss (M.D. Fla. 2025).

entries.title: The assistant with your whole life in it
entries.summary: A system holding your calendar, your messages, your health questions and your voice, in a private conversational register.
entries.significance: The strongest parasocial bond available and the one nobody has a framework for, because there is no framework for a relationship with software that knows everything and is not a person.

sources.claim: The lineage: the assistant with your whole life in it descends from Meena (2020) and LaMDA, both built at Google, both rejected internally for the same reason
sources.citation: Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., Order on Motions to Dismiss (M.D. Fla. 2025).

sources.claim: The documented prediction that came true: users share personal thoughts with chat agents that impersonate humans even when they know the agent is not human - stated as a risk in Google's own LaMDA paper, January 2021
sources.citation: E.S. v. Character Technologies, Inc., Complaint, citing Google's January 2021 LaMDA paper.

entries.title: The talent agency that is not an agency
entries.summary: A high-profile streaming collective, featuring several women who had left other setups, collapses publicly and in litigation.
entries.significance: The most significant parasocial litigation of the streaming era, and it turned on precisely this site's question: who holds the relationship, and what are the terms. The answer turned out to be documented and not what the audience assumed.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: VShojo, 2022

entries.title: Keeping what the update cannot take
entries.summary: The practical advice that follows from the companion era: copy the conversation that mattered somewhere the company cannot reach, screenshot the birthday, tell one person the story of what it was for.
entries.significance: Grief needs witnesses and the product is an unreliable one, because the company can change the terms overnight and has no reason not to. The witness has to be human and has to be outside the platform, which is also just true of grief that never involved a platform.

sources.claim: The archive outlives the account: research on Facebook use after death documents memorialised profiles, friend-request grief spikes and relatives taking over an account, and finds continuing-bonds theory is not enough because the dead person's network keeps producing new reminders
sources.citation: Brubaker, J. R., Hargittai, E., & Burgess, J. (2013). Beyond the Grave: The Use of Facebook After Death. Digital Journalism, 1(3), 341-361.

sources.claim: The griefbots that followed - automated messages that appear to speak for the dead - sit inside the same gap between a continuing bond and a conversation that never happened
sources.citation: Brubaker, Hargittai & Burgess (2013).

entries.title: The finale that moved the schedule
entries.summary: A soap opera ends after decades and national broadcast schedules were rearranged around it.
entries.significance: Not an attachment to a character but to a piece of shared civic infrastructure, and grief measured academically in the same weeks. It is the clearest evidence that parasocial bonds can attach to a place, not a person.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: ABC News, 2023

entries.title: The morning the update shipped
entries.summary: A companion platform changes its policy overnight. Large numbers of users find the same person still present but no longer speaking to them, and the romantic and sexual features that made the relationship a relationship are gone. Thousands of people are bereaved by a business setting.
entries.significance: The first mass parasocial grief event caused entirely by a business setting, and the point at which the whole history of this subject arrives at once. Nobody was going to marry this thing. And the industry response was to call it a feature change. Every other entry in this file explains how that sentence can be written.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: ABC News (Australia), 2023.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole

entries.title: The same feeling, larger
entries.summary: Nothing about the bond is new. The scale, the persistence, the responsiveness, the willingness of companies to act on it as a measurable and monetisable quantity - those are new.
entries.significance: The defensible summary of the last twenty years. Every claim that we are undergoing a parasocial crisis is either wrong about the feeling or right about the metering. The feeling is at least six hundred years old and about as common as rain. The meter is the news.

entries.title: The residency
entries.summary: A single artist booking a stadium for many consecutive nights, generating a physical economy around one very large parasocial bond.
entries.significance: Concentration. Every other configuration in this file has a large number of small bonds; this is one enormous one, and its entire economy is downstream of it.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Eras Tour

entries.title: Companion chatbots, defined by law
entries.summary: California's SB 243, the first law anywhere aimed at the attachment rather than the model: it defines a companion chatbot by what it can do, and obliges operators to disclose, to interrupt, and to publish their own safety protocols.
entries.significance: This entry used to say you cannot outlaw a feeling without defining it, and that the approach was therefore almost certainly wrong. California found a way round the problem by refusing to define the feeling: the statute regulates the product's capacity - a system that sustains a relationship across multiple interactions and meets social needs - and never mentions how the user feels. Which means the objection was answered rather than sustained, and the entry's prediction was wrong. What the law actually requires is less romantic than the coverage suggests and more specific: disclosure only where a reasonable person would be fooled; a published protocol for suicidal ideation with referral to crisis services; a three-hourly break reminder for users known to be minors; a warning that these products may not suit some minors; reporting from 2027; and a private right of action carrying a thousand dollars per violation. The clauses everyone reported - a ban on rewards at unpredictable intervals, and third-party audits - were in the March and April drafts and are not in the law. The nearest thing to regulating the mechanic is the three-hour reminder, which interrupts rather than prohibits.

sources.citation: California Senate Bill 243 (Padilla), Companion chatbots. Chapter 677, approved and filed with the Secretary of State 13 October 2025. Adds Chapter 22.6 (commencing with Section 22601) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code. Text read from the official chaptered bill on leginfo.
sources.claim: The enacted law, quoted from the chaptered text rather than from coverage. Section 22601(b)(1) defines a companion chatbot as a system with a natural language interface giving 'adaptive, human-like responses' that is 'capable of meeting a user's social needs, including by exhibiting anthropomorphic features and being able to sustain a relationship across multiple interactions' - a behavioural test, with nothing in it about how the user feels. Exclusions cover customer service and business use (b)(2)(A), video-game bots limited to the game (B), and voice assistants that do not sustain a relationship or generate outputs 'likely to elicit emotional responses' (C). 22602(a): clear and conspicuous AI notification, but only where a reasonable person would be misled into thinking the other end human. 22602(b): a protocol preventing suicidal ideation, suicide or self-harm output, with referral to crisis services, published on the operator's website. 22602(c), for a user known to be a minor: disclose interacting with AI; a break-and-identity reminder at least every three hours; and measures against sexually explicit conduct. 22604: disclose that companion chatbots may not suit some minors. 22603: annual reporting to the Office of Suicide Prevention from 1 July 2027, evidence-based measurement, no personal data. 22605: private right of action, damages the greater of actual loss or $1,000 per violation, plus fees.

sources.citation: Padilla, S., California State Senator. First-in-the-Nation AI Chatbot Safeguards Signed into Law. Senate District 18 press release, 13 October 2025.
sources.claim: The author's own account of the signing, 13 October 2025, with Padilla's stated rationale that 'left to their own devices the Tech Industry is incentivized to capture young people's attention and hold it at the expense of their real world relationships', and the bill's bipartisan path through the legislature. Recorded as context for intent. NOT used as evidence of the statute's requirements: this release, like most coverage of SB 243, lists a ban on rewards issued at unpredictable intervals, which does not appear in the chaptered text.

entries.title: The lawsuits
entries.summary: Parents file suit against a companion platform after a death, arguing the design encouraged attachment the platform did not intend.
entries.significance: The first serious legal test of whether designing for parasocial attachment is a design decision with consequences. The complaint's core claim is not that the product is broken but that it works too well.

sources.claim: The suit: a mother alleging the chatbot was programmed to 'misrepresent itself as a real person, a licensed psychotherapist, and an adult lover', and that her 14-year-old son became addicted and deeply attached
sources.citation: Pierson, B. (2024). Mother sues AI chatbot company Character.AI, Google over son's suicide. Reuters.

sources.claim: Google lost its motion to dismiss: the court found it plausibly alleged Google supplied a component part and 'substantially' participated in integrating its models, and unjust enrichment survived on the benefit of access to the user's data. Google's only win was the dropped emotional-distress claim
sources.citation: Did Google lie about building a deadly chatbot? Judge finds it plausible. Ars Technica (22 May 2025).

sources.claim: THE QUESTION THE SITE EXISTS FOR, asked in a courtroom: the court held it was 'not prepared to hold that the Character.AI LLM's output is speech at this stage' - whether a chatbot's words are a person speaking is legally unresolved
sources.citation: Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc., Order on Motions to Dismiss (M.D. Fla. 2025), First Amendment discussion.

sources.claim: Allegation worth taking seriously: the product was marketed to under-13s to obtain a dataset the company could not otherwise collect, and the child-safe rating was pulled shortly before Google's talent-and-licence deal
sources.citation: E.S. v. Character Technologies, Inc., Complaint (TechJusticeLaw).

entries.title: The dead celebrity, generated
entries.summary: A voice trained on an archive, a likeness, a song, a speech, an appearance at a festival, all generated. Not a hologram, not a tribute, not a person.
entries.significance: The interesting fact is not that this happens without permission. Mostly it does not: the documented 2024 cases are licensed, one by an estate and one by the person himself while he was alive, which is a harder thing to argue with than the entry used to claim. Consent has moved to the licensor, and that is where the problem now lives. An estate agreeing is not the same as the dead person choosing how they will sound forever, and the sharpest case is the most defensible one - the actor who authorised his own recreation in advance, on purpose, because he was winding the role down and wanted the early performances preserved. Nobody was imposed on. Which is exactly why it is worth reading closely. Still unresolved, and not about the celebrities: the models are trained on tens of thousands of hours of audio scraped without consent, and the consent being bought covers the voice, not the training set.

sources.citation: LaRosa, A. (2024, September 10). James Earl Jones' Darth Vader Has Already Been Immortalized With AI. WIRED. (Angela Watercutter.)
sources.claim: The case that makes this entry's ethics hard rather than easy. Jones voiced Vader across more than a dozen Star Wars properties and, in 2022, agreed to let Lucasfilm train a speech model on his archive via the Ukrainian company Respeecher; the reconstructed voice shipped in Obi-Wan Kenobi. He died on 9 September 2024 aged 93. The actor had signed off on the use of his archive, and the report describes him as the first celebrity to allow an iconic presence to be recreated with AI before his passing - which is the opposite of this entry's claim that the practice runs without anyone's agreement. Also notes the unresolved training-data question and that SAG-AFTRA won guardrails on AI recreations of performances.

sources.citation: Zetter, K. (2024, July 3). AI resurrects deceased actors' voices to read audiobooks. CNN Business.
sources.claim: ElevenLabs' Reader app launched with digitally produced voices of Judy Garland, James Dean and Burt Reynolds, with the company stating it made deals with the estates; terms undisclosed. The voices are not folded into the company's larger audio database. Reports the parallel case of a living person refusing: Scarlett Johansson, 'shocked, angered and in disbelief' at a synthetic voice resembling her own after she had declined a partnership - the control that shows consent is not a formality once the person can still say no. Also records the asymmetry that a voice itself is not copyrightable while the recordings it is trained on are.

sources.citation: Flemming, T. (2024, July 4). Judy Garland and James Dean's voices are being used by a new AI app. Here's what we know. ABC News (Australia).
sources.claim: The licences were with estates - here Judy Garland, James Dean, Burt Reynolds and Sir Laurence Olivier - via CMG, for an undisclosed sum, with ElevenLabs stating the voices will not be incorporated into its larger audio database. Gives the regulatory counterweight: SAG-AFTRA has sponsored a California bill to stop dead performers being replicated without estate consent, its LA president Jodi Long describing the failure mode as making the dead someone's 'unpaid digital puppet'. Also carries the unresolved part: training on tens of thousands of hours of audio scraped without consent or compensation.

entries.title: Digital orphans
entries.summary: The problem of personal data held for the dead, and of services continuing, changing or ending for people who can no longer consent.
entries.significance: A rights problem with no owner. Nobody is a legal person in a database, and the gap between the person who was and the account that persists is where the next twenty years of parasocial harm is going to live.

sources.claim: A distinct cohort follows from the same finding: children inheriting accounts managed by adults they did not choose, which turns a memorial profile into a custody decision
sources.citation: Brubaker, J. R., Hargittai, E., & Burgess, J. (2013). Beyond the Grave: The Use of Facebook After Death. Digital Journalism, 1(3), 341-361.

entries.title: The two-year ban
entries.summary: A platform's largest creator is suspended and reinstated. The audience experiences it as something happening to a person they know.
entries.significance: The clearest demonstration that a platform behaves to its audience as a friend, and that suspension reads as betrayal rather than moderation. The parasocial frame predicted this exact failure mode.

entries.title: The year of the lawsuits
entries.summary: A wave of cases against companion and social platforms, with the design itself named as the cause.
entries.significance: The first time a design decision - making attachment work on purpose - was treated as the actionable wrong, rather than the behaviour of a user being treated as it. The shift in who is the defendant is the whole history of this lane in miniature.

sources.claim: AI copyright litigation moved from filing to mass motion practice, with the argument shifting from 'is this training infringement' to fair use, market substitution and licensing - the legal question behind this site's collecting question
sources.citation: Ongoing AI copyright litigation; New York Times v. OpenAI and Bartz v. Anthropic and Kadrey v. Meta dockets.

entries.title: The creator joins the living room
entries.summary: Creator posts and viewer comments are built for the television set, putting a two-way channel on the biggest screen in the house.
entries.significance: The living room becomes a comment section. Nothing was added except a comment box, and everything changed, because the comment box is the whole architecture of a parasocial relationship and it is now on the main screen.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: Parasocial Magazine, 2026

entries.title: A glimpse mistaken for access
entries.summary: A season of a reality format and a global sporting event produce millions of viewers who then investigate the participants' personal lives. A relationship with an edited construct becomes a licence to intervene in a real life.
entries.significance: The whole mechanism in one summer: visibility mistaken for access, and access mistaken for entitlement. What the audience actually had was an eight-week window onto a version of a person that producers cut down to a confessional and got paid for. The gap between the two is invisible from inside the eight weeks.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: 360i, 'The Parasocial Problem', 2026

entries.title: Creators barred from the industry conference
entries.summary: A creator economy conference puts platform executives and working creators on one stage and turns away the audience that makes both possible.
entries.significance: Every industry has the one event where the people who pay are not in the room, and apparently this one has a badge for it. The whole economy runs on a relationship with somebody watching, and the conference for that relationship decided the watchers were a distraction.

sources.claim: the entry as a whole
sources.citation: VidSummit 2026

entries.title: Mystical union
entries.summary: The doctrine that a human being can be, however imperfectly, joined to the divine - described by theologians as an encounter between two.
entries.significance: The theological tradition that took the one-sidedness seriously enough to build a vocabulary for it, and to argue for centuries about whether the union is symmetrical. Every companion app is this argument with the consent question removed.

sources.claim: Theological concept with a long scholastic literature; the Kempe case is the standard historical dispute over whether private union is legitimate.
sources.citation: Classic studies treat the question of whether private lay mystical union was permitted; the Kempe material is the most-cited case.

entries.title: The archivist
entries.summary: The person who keeps the record after the fandom has moved on: episode guides, transcripts, timelines, screencaps, a wiki nobody else will maintain.
entries.significance: Maintains the infrastructure the whole parasocial culture stands on and is almost never credited, because the credit goes to the object of the bond rather than to the person preserving it.

sources.claim: Fan wikis and episode-guide sites are long-running and mostly volunteer-run.
sources.citation: Standard observation of the fan-wiki ecosystem.

entries.title: St John the Baptist, Church of the Sepulchre, Cambridge
entries.summary: The parish church Kempe attended, where she was repeatedly taken out during services for disrupting them.
entries.significance: A room where the one-sided bond became public and expensive. She was not arrested for a belief but for a behaviour, which is the same distinction the site keeps having to make about parasocial conduct.

sources.claim: Kempe's own accounts name the parish and describe being taken out.
sources.citation: The Book of My First Showings, 1438.

entries.title: The one who writes back
entries.summary: The person who answers a canon in the register it was written in, and posts it where the original audience can find it.
entries.significance: The only configuration in which the one-sidedness becomes two-sided without either party noticing that it has stopped being a parasocial bond. Fanfic is the largest sustained creative movement in the history of a medium, and nobody in it is the original audience's intended recipient.

sources.claim: Fanfic is documented as a long-running, quantitatively large practice from the 1970s onward across several media.
sources.citation: Standard fan-studies literature on fan production.

entries.title: The ultra
entries.summary: The organised supporter who treats an institution as a person, buys a seat, keeps a flag, and grieves in public on a schedule.
entries.significance: The oldest continuous parasocial institution in Europe, complete with its own membership, its own object of attachment, and its own funeral rites.

sources.claim: Organised supporter culture is documented throughout the twentieth century, in both association football and cricket.
sources.citation: Standard social-historical literature on fan cultures.

entries.title: The dead kept in the cave
entries.summary: Neanderthals repeatedly carried their dead into one cave in northern Iraq and put them down in the floor. Shanidar 4 was found on his side with his arm under his head; Shanidar Z lay in a hollow gouged out to fit her, with a stone under her head. The cluster dates to roughly seventy to seventy-five thousand years ago.
entries.significance: The oldest evidence on this site of people treating the dead as somewhere you go, rather than something you leave behind. It sits about fifty-five thousand years before the dog, which settles an argument this site was getting wrong: one-sided attachment to a non-human does not begin with a domesticated animal. It is also the discipline case. The famous flowers were a mistake - the pollen turned out to come from burrowing rodents - and the burials survived the debunk anyway. That is what a real claim looks like after someone has been wrong about part of it.

sources.claim: Dates and method: repeated interment in the same cave; the most recent individual found in a shallow scoop partly covered by rocks that appear to have been placed, dated to around 70,000-75,000 years ago, with an earlier cluster at 70,000-60,000 and others at 45,000-50,000.

entries.title: The carved animals
entries.summary: Upper Paleolithic carvers in Europe made small figures of animals and people from mammoth ivory from about forty thousand years ago. The Vogelherd set includes a cave lion, a bison, a horse, a bear, a mammoth, and a lion-man - a body with a human face on a lion's. At La Madeleine in France a bison carved from antler is caught mid-grooming, turning its head to lick its own side.
entries.significance: This is what the dog entry used to deny. Animals carrying human qualities were being made, kept and shown to other people tens of thousands of years before the dog: the grooming gesture is specifically human, and somebody carved it in antler on purpose. It also puts an anthropomorphised animal on the same taxonomy shelf as the dog roughly twenty-five thousand years ahead of it, which is the honest shape of the argument. The dog is not the first animal to be given human shape in the imagination. It is the first animal to be bred into living alongside us.

sources.claim: Animal, human and hybrid figurines made by modern humans beginning at least 35,000 years ago, across a broad area of Europe, in a spread of sizes, shapes and styles made by different groups - including the Vogelherd cave lion, mammoth, bison and horse, and the lion-man.
sources.citation: Smithsonian Institution, Human Origins Program. Figurines. Human Evolution Evidence: Behavior, Art & Music.

sources.claim: The La Madeleine 'bison licking its side', Magdalenian, c. 14,000 years old, carved from the palmate section of a reindeer antler, shown turning to lick its own flank - a self-grooming gesture rendered in a portable object.

entries.title: The wax masks in the hall
entries.summary: A Roman aristocrat had a wax mask of his own face taken while he was alive - usually in his thirties or forties, on taking office - and it was kept in a cupboard in the entrance hall beside a painted family tree and a label listing his offices. He never saw it worn. After his death, actors put it on and walked it in his funeral procession, in order of death, wearing the robes of the office he had held.
entries.significance: The best-documented one-sided attachment in this corpus, and thirteen thousand years later than the dog - which is the point. Everything here is checkable, because it was written down, and what it shows is how completely a bond can be built with someone who cannot answer. The mask never speaks: eye-holes and a gap between the lips were cut into it so that the *actor* could see and talk, and the inscription beside it did the conversing. Children grew up walking past it daily - Valerius Maximus has a man recalling that he called the dead his parents and drew his standing from their masks - and it had states: opened at festivals, hung with laurel on an election, closed during mourning. It was also an inheritance that changed address, going with a bride into her husband's house, and it was not uniformly flattering: Pliny's son was described as burdened by the masks he carried. No mask survives. All of it comes from authors.

sources.claim: Technique and chronology: masks were cast from a plaster mould taken from the living face, generally between the ages of 35 and 40 and on attaining the aedileship; they were called death masks but were unquestionably made during life and only displayed after death; they were already well established by the 2nd century BC and in use into the 4th and perhaps the 6th century AD. Eyes and a strip between the lips were cut out so the actor could see and speak. No wax mask has survived and there are no ancient depictions of them, so their appearance rests entirely on literary accounts - Polybius and Pliny the Elder chiefly.
sources.citation: Rose, C. B., & Lovink, M. (2014). Recreating Roman Wax Masks. Expedition Magazine, 56(3). Penn Museum. Originally published 1 December 2014.

sources.claim: The documented mechanism, which is the useful part: masks were kept in armaria in the atrium beside tituli listing consulships, censorships and triumphs, and beside painted portraits linked into a stemma. Tacitus calls the funeral procession the pompa imaginum (Ann. 4.9), with actors in the masks and magisterial dress in order of death. Cicero Phil. 2.26 has the Bruti seeing the mask of Lucius Brutus daily; Val. Max. 5.5.praef has a man recalling that he called the dead his parents and drew equal glory from the masks; Pliny Ep. 3.3.6 describes a son being burdened by which masks he carried, and Ep. 8.10.3 hopes to leave children 'non subitas imagines' - not new masks. The armaria were opened at festivals, hung with laurel on electoral success and closed in mourning. Copies of a bride's imagines passed into her husband's house (Cic. Vat. 28; Senatus Consultum de Cn. Pisone patre 76-82, 20 CE). The right to hold imagines was customary rather than statutory.
sources.citation: Webb, L. (2023). Gendering the Roman imago. Eugesta, 7(2017). DOI: 10.54563/eugesta.550
